meta.blurb: Orla Venn goes down to the cellar for one special bottle of wine and never comes back. When the lights fail, her guests find the door bolted from outside. The sea has cut off the island, and the killer is here.
meta.bible: Ines Calloway: an insurance investigator in her thirties, calm, observant and stubborn; she comes to value the lodge's paintings and tells the story as it happens. Orla Venn: the seventy-year-old owner of Tern Rock Lodge, sharp and warm; she is selling the lodge; she is found dead in the cellar. Felix Venn: Orla's nephew, charming, in debt; he searches the study at night looking for her new will. Hugh Marlowe: Orla's accountant, nervous; he has been borrowing from her account and plans to repay it. Dr Priya Nair: Orla's doctor and old friend, calm and clear. Gideon Frost: an elderly painter and friend of Orla, grumpy; he painted The Grey Heron and knows its secret, a tiny white fleck in the heron's eye. Lucas Reyes: a smooth art dealer, the buyer's agent; he stole the real painting and killed Orla in the cellar. Tamsin Reed: a young journalist writing about the lodge; she is shut in the cold store. Marta Okoye: Orla's lawyer, who knows the new will: the lodge goes to the island's lifeboat. Mr Bell: the caretaker and boatman, steady and practical; his boat is wrecked in the storm. Mrs Bright: the cook, who notices everything. Tern Rock Lodge: an old stone hotel on a small island, reached by a causeway that floods at high tide. The Grey Heron: the lodge's most valuable painting, hung in the study; the hanging copy has no fleck in the eye. Reyes Fine Art: Lucas's gallery, named on a label found in the cellar. Facts: the cellar door has a bolt on the outside; Orla's watch stopped at 8.58; the lights failed at 9.05; the cellar is at the back, past the kitchen; the cloakroom is at the front; low tide opens the causeway about 4.40 on Sunday morning. Voice and tone: tense, fair and clear, a puzzle told step by step; the death is stated plainly with no gore; every clue is shown to the reader. ADDITIONS FOR THE FULL BOOK. Ines Calloway: she served six years in the police before six years as an insurance investigator; she carries a small magnifying glass and a heavy torch. Captain Arthur Venn: Orla's late husband, who led the Tern Rock Lifeboat crew for thirty years and wound the hall clock every Friday; the clock has a little door in its case. Tern Rock Lifeboat: the island's lifeboat, whose crew Orla wants to help; the lodge will go to the Lifeboat under the new will, signed two weeks ago. The Boathouse: a stone building by the Jetty where Mr Bell's blue boat is kept. The Jetty: a stone pier in the small harbour. Sunday: the day the sea road opens again. Felix, Hugh, Gideon and Lucas came on Thursday; Dr Priya, Marta and Tamsin came on Friday. The Visitors' Book: kept in the hall. Rooms: the Hall, the Lounge, the Study, the Library, the Dining Room (two doors: one to the Hall, one at the back to the kitchen passage), the Kitchen, the Cloakroom (at the front), the Cellar (at the back), the Cold Store, the Attic. Seating at dinner: Orla at the head, Marta on her right, Ines between Gideon and Dr Priya, Felix opposite Ines, Lucas, Hugh and Tamsin in the other places. The cellar key hangs on a hook by the back door of the dining room. Mrs Bright keeps candles and matches on a dresser in the kitchen passage. Orla left the table at a quarter to nine; Lucas left a few minutes later; Mrs Bright heard a thump from the back passage at 8.58 by the kitchen clock; the lights failed at 9.05 when the storm broke the power line. More facts of the full book. The Heron was stolen on Thursday night: Lucas lifted the real canvas from its frame, rolled it into a stout cardboard tube and hung a copy painted in a week by a forger in the city; the copy came in a gold frame labelled Reyes Fine Art, which he hid under a white sheet in the cellar behind the wine racks; the copy has no fleck and has a pale modern stretcher, bright tacks and fresh varnish; Lucas measured the Heron three weeks ago (the Visitors' Book). Orla found the gold frame at four on Friday afternoon and came up pale; at dinner she looked at Lucas; she went down again at a quarter to nine and Lucas followed her; at the cellar door she said she would call the police; he pushed her down the steps, bolted the door, and stood in the dark scullery until the lights failed at 9.05; he took a candle from the dresser in the passage and came into the Dining Room from the Hall door. The cellar walls are whitewashed and there is a grating high in the back wall; a white smear on Lucas's cuff; a scrape in the whitewash at shoulder height. Mrs Bright saw him come out of the passage with a lit candle. Tamsin's recorder on the dinner table shows Lucas silent from ten to nine until the lights fail and a thump at 8.58. Saturday: Gideon sees the copy; Felix admits he searched for the will (he owes a large debt); Marta says the new will leaves the lodge to the Tern Rock Lifeboat; Dr Priya says Orla had a weak heart and perhaps a year; Hugh admits borrowing from Orla's money; Lucas hides the tube in the clock early Saturday (Tamsin sees him), Tamsin finds it that dusk and is pushed into the Cold Store with a chair wedged under the handle; Lucas then hides the tube in Mr Bell's wrecked boat in the Boathouse. Ines announces at supper that Mr Bell will fetch the police at first light; Lucas fetches the tube at three on Sunday morning; the sea road shows at about 4.20 and Lucas is caught on it by Ines, Felix and Mr Bell; Felix tears the tube from his hands. The police arrive at sunrise. Orla's will names the lifeboat as heir because its crew carried Arthur's coffin ten years ago.

beats.scene: Ines stands on a windy shore with her suitcase, facing a distant island
beats.summary: Ines Calloway reaches the shore opposite Tern Rock on Friday afternoon with a case and a commission.

beats.scene: A battered old car rattles up and a broad man leans out
beats.summary: Mr Bell, the caretaker and boatman, arrives to carry her across and warns that the sea road is open only at low tide.

beats.scene: Tall white posts stand in the sand beside a wet stone causeway
beats.summary: Mr Bell explains the tide posts and how the causeway floods twice a day.

beats.scene: The old car crosses the causeway with waves close on both sides
beats.summary: They cross the causeway, with the wet sand shining and dark cloud piling on the horizon.

beats.scene: A grey stone lodge with tall chimneys on a small rocky island
beats.summary: Tern Rock Lodge comes into view, with its chimneys, its small harbour and its stone jetty.

beats.scene: Gulls wheel above a stone jetty, a boathouse and a small blue boat
beats.summary: Mr Bell points out his boat and the boathouse, the island's only way off at high water.

beats.scene: Orla Venn waits at the lodge door, leaning on a silver-topped stick
beats.summary: Orla Venn welcomes Ines on the doorstep, small and upright, with bright quick eyes.

beats.scene: A busy hall with a tall clock, a coat stand and a wide staircase
beats.summary: Orla leads Ines into the hall, where voices drift from the lounge, and says who else has come.

beats.scene: Mrs Bright pours tea in a warm kitchen with a black iron stove
beats.summary: Mrs Bright, the cook, gives Ines tea and says the larder is full in case the storm keeps them in.

beats.scene: Orla speaks quietly to Ines in a corner of the busy hall
beats.summary: Orla says she is selling the lodge and asks Ines to examine the paintings and tell her the truth.

beats.scene: Orla rests her hand on the case of a tall grandfather clock
beats.summary: Orla shows Ines the grandfather clock, which her husband wound every Friday and which has never lost a minute.

beats.scene: A small study lined with books, with a large painting over the fireplace
beats.summary: Orla opens the study and shows Ines her best painting, The Grey Heron, above the fire.

beats.scene: A lone grey bird stands in shallow water at dawn
beats.summary: Orla describes the Heron and says it is worth more than the island and every stone on it.

beats.scene: Two men drink tea by a log fire in the lounge
beats.summary: Ines meets Felix, Orla's charming nephew, who is elegant, cheerful and tired around the eyes.

beats.scene: A nervous man in glasses taps his fingers on an account book
beats.summary: Ines meets Hugh Marlowe, Orla's anxious accountant, who cannot stop talking about the sale.

beats.scene: A woman with a small black bag sits calmly beside the fire
beats.summary: Ines meets Dr Priya Nair, Orla's doctor and oldest friend, who speaks softly and listens closely.

beats.scene: An old painter with paint-stained fingers glares at the sea view
beats.summary: Ines meets Gideon Frost, the old painter of The Grey Heron, who is grumpy and honest.

beats.scene: A man in a pale suit shakes hands with a smile
beats.summary: Ines meets Lucas Reyes, a smooth art dealer who acts for the buyer of the lodge.

beats.scene: A young woman in a coat writes in a notebook beside a window
beats.summary: Ines meets Tamsin Reed, a young journalist, and Marta Okoye, Orla's careful lawyer.

beats.scene: Mr Bell stands at a window pointing at heavy clouds over the sea
beats.summary: Mr Bell warns that a storm is coming and that the sea road will soon close.

beats.scene: Ines follows Mrs Bright up a staircase hung with sea paintings
beats.summary: Mrs Bright shows Ines to her room along a staircase hung with paintings of the coast.

beats.scene: A small bedroom with a narrow bed and a window on the sea
beats.summary: Ines unpacks in a small room that overlooks the jetty and the sea road, and sets her torch by the bed.

beats.scene: A row of small oil paintings on a landing, with a lamp beside them
beats.summary: Ines examines the lesser paintings on the landing and finds them old, dusty and honest.

beats.scene: Lifeboat men in oilskins stand beside a lifeboat in a framed old snapshot
beats.summary: A faded snapshot shows Captain Arthur Venn, Orla's late husband, and his lifeboat crew.

beats.scene: Ines holds a lamp close to the large heron painting in the study
beats.summary: Ines returns alone to the study and looks at The Grey Heron, and thinks the varnish looks strangely new.

beats.scene: A finger hovers over a glossy patch of paint on a canvas
beats.summary: The varnish smells fresh and shines too brightly, but Ines tells herself she is no expert.

beats.scene: Orla comes into the study, tapping her stick on the floor
beats.summary: Orla finds Ines in the study and asks her to look at the Heron again tomorrow, in daylight.

beats.scene: Rain begins to streak a dark window as the wind rattles the glass
beats.summary: The storm arrives, and the guests gather in the lounge as the light fades.

beats.scene: Waves crash over the causeway as rain streaks a dark window
beats.summary: The sea covers the causeway and Mr Bell says that no one can leave tonight.

beats.scene: A man holds a dead black telephone in a dim hallway
beats.summary: The telephone goes dead and mobile phones have no signal, so the island is cut off before dinner.

beats.scene: A long dining table laid with silver, candles and bowls of soup
beats.summary: The guests take their seats for dinner, and Mrs Bright serves hot soup.

beats.scene: Name cards stand beside each plate on a long white tablecloth
beats.summary: Orla sits at the head of the table, and Ines is placed between Gideon and Dr Priya.

beats.scene: Hugh talks quickly with his hands above a plate of soup
beats.summary: Hugh talks about money and the sale until Orla gently asks him to stop.

beats.scene: Gideon points a fork at his plate and scowls
beats.summary: Gideon complains about modern art, Lucas smooths the quarrel, and Tamsin asks too many questions.

beats.scene: Orla stands at the head of the table with a glass in her hand
beats.summary: Orla announces to everyone that she is selling the lodge to a buyer from abroad.

beats.scene: Felix pushes back his chair and glares at his aunt
beats.summary: Felix is furious, because he has always expected to inherit the lodge.

beats.scene: Marta rests her hand on a folder while the table goes quiet
beats.summary: Marta says nothing, Dr Priya calms the table, and Orla promises him a quiet talk later.

beats.scene: The tall clock in the hall shows a quarter to nine
beats.summary: At a quarter to nine Orla says she will fetch a very special bottle of wine for a toast.

beats.scene: Orla lifts a key from a hook and walks into a dim passage
beats.summary: Orla takes the cellar key from its hook and walks along the kitchen passage.

beats.scene: A pale man in a hat slips away from a crowded dining table
beats.summary: Lucas leaves the table to wash his hands, while Hugh talks about money and Mrs Bright serves the main course.

beats.scene: Candles gutter on a long table while the wind howls outside
beats.summary: The main course is served, the toast waits, and Gideon grumbles that the bottle is taking very long.

beats.scene: Mrs Bright pauses at the kitchen door with her head tilted
beats.summary: Mrs Bright hears a dull thump from the back passage and decides it is only the storm.

beats.scene: The grandfather clock shows nine as guests glance at an empty chair
beats.summary: The clock strikes nine, Orla is still not back, and Dr Priya begins to look worried.

beats.scene: Every light in the dining room goes out at once
beats.summary: At five past nine the lights fail and the room falls black.

beats.scene: A pale hand holding a lit candle appears in the hall doorway
beats.summary: Lucas comes back into the room carrying a lit candle and says he was in the cloakroom.

beats.scene: Mr Bell lifts a lamp beside a fuse box on a stone wall
beats.summary: Mr Bell checks the fuse box and finds it sound, so the storm has cut the power line.

beats.scene: An empty chair stands beside a candle that burns low
beats.summary: Ines asks where Orla is, and no one has seen her for twenty minutes.

beats.scene: Ines and Mr Bell carry candles along a dark stone passage
beats.summary: Ines and Mr Bell go to look for Orla and follow the kitchen passage towards the cellar.

beats.scene: A heavy cellar door with a bolt on its outer side stands in candlelight
beats.summary: They find the cellar door bolted from the outside.

beats.scene: Ines slides back the bolt and candlelight falls on a still figure below
beats.summary: Orla lies at the foot of the cellar steps.

beats.scene: A doctor kneels beside a still figure at the foot of the cellar steps
beats.summary: Dr Priya examines Orla and says that she is dead.

beats.scene: Candlelight on a cracked watch on a thin wrist
beats.summary: Ines notices that Orla's watch has stopped at two minutes to nine.

beats.scene: A doctor's finger rests near a bruise on a shoulder
beats.summary: Dr Priya says the fall killed Orla, but a bruise on her shoulder looks like the mark of a hard shove.

beats.scene: Ines looks closely at the iron bolt on the cellar door
beats.summary: Ines points out that no one could bolt the door from inside, so it was not an accident.

beats.scene: A brass key lies on the second cellar step in the candlelight
beats.summary: Ines finds the cellar key on the steps, where Orla dropped it after unlocking the door herself.

beats.scene: Eight guests stand pale and silent in the lounge as rain hammers the windows
beats.summary: Ines tells the guests that she must treat this as a crime, since the island is cut off from help.

beats.scene: Felix shouts while Gideon scoffs and Marta stares at Ines
beats.summary: Ines explains that she was a police officer for six years before she joined the insurers.

beats.scene: Mr Bell stands on a wet jetty beside a broken boat
beats.summary: Mr Bell finds his boat smashed by the storm, so there is no way off the island.

beats.scene: A radio set with a cracked case and a puddle of water
beats.summary: Mr Bell's radio is ruined by seawater, so there is no way to call for help.

beats.scene: Ines locks the cellar door and puts the key in her pocket
beats.summary: Ines covers Orla with a blanket, locks the cellar and keeps the key.

beats.scene: Ines writes in her notebook while guests sit in different corners
beats.summary: Ines asks everyone where they were at two minutes to nine, and she writes down every answer.

beats.scene: Hugh and Dr Priya sit side by side, speaking one after the other
beats.summary: Hugh and Dr Priya both say they never left their chairs, and nobody contradicts them.

beats.scene: Lucas lounges in an armchair and smiles at the notebook
beats.summary: Lucas says he was in the cloakroom at that moment, and nobody saw where he went.

beats.scene: A pencil plan of the lodge with the cellar marked at the back
beats.summary: Ines sees that the cloakroom is at the front of the lodge and the cellar at the back.

beats.scene: A list of names in a notebook, with a line beside each
beats.summary: Ines writes down who would gain from Orla's death, and finds three or four names.

beats.scene: Mr Bell tries the locked back door by lantern light
beats.summary: Mr Bell and Ines check every door and window and find that no stranger came in.

beats.scene: Guests pick at a cold supper without speaking
beats.summary: Nobody eats, so Ines asks everyone to lock their doors and not to wander alone.

beats.scene: Ines sits on her bed turning an old iron bolt over in her mind
beats.summary: Alone in her room, Ines thinks about the bolt and who in the lodge was strong enough to push Orla.

beats.scene: A floorboard creaks and a torch beam moves along a dark landing
beats.summary: At midnight Ines hears footsteps below and creeps downstairs with her torch.

beats.scene: A man in a bright jacket kneels at a desk opening drawers
beats.summary: In the study Ines finds Felix searching the desk, and he runs off into the dark.

beats.scene: Grey light creeps over wet windows and a tray of cold tea
beats.summary: Saturday dawns grey and rainy, and the guests come down to a silent breakfast.

beats.scene: Felix sits with his head in his hands in the grey morning light
beats.summary: Felix admits that he was looking for the new will, because he owes a lot of money.

beats.scene: A thin man signs a paper while another man looks on
beats.summary: Felix says he owes a dangerous sum, which his aunt refused to pay last month.

beats.scene: Ines frowns at a notebook, weighing one name against another
beats.summary: Ines decides that Felix has a motive, but also a reason to keep his aunt alive until she changed her mind.

beats.scene: A lawyer holds a folded paper in a quiet corner of the library
beats.summary: Marta tells Ines that Orla's new will leaves the lodge to the island's lifeboat, with little for Felix.

beats.scene: Marta takes a signed letter from her case and lays it on a desk
beats.summary: Marta explains that Orla signed the will two weeks ago and meant to tell Felix gently after dinner.

beats.scene: Dr Priya sits beside a window with her black bag on her lap
beats.summary: Dr Priya says Orla had a weak heart and perhaps a year to live, and that is why she was selling.

beats.scene: Hugh Marlowe sweats over an open account book at a small table
beats.summary: Hugh admits he has been borrowing money from Orla's account but says he was at dinner all evening.

beats.scene: A cook in a white apron stands firmly by a pile of dishes
beats.summary: Mrs Bright confirms that Hugh never left his chair all evening, because she served him twice.

beats.scene: Ines stands alone at the study door looking at the large painting
beats.summary: Ines remembers that Orla asked her to look at the Heron by daylight, and goes in.

beats.scene: An old painter stares at the heron painting with his nose almost touching it
beats.summary: Gideon looks at The Grey Heron in the morning light and says it is not his painting.

beats.scene: Gideon sits down heavily on a chair in front of a dim painting
beats.summary: Gideon says that he painted the Heron forty years ago in a rented room by the sea.

beats.scene: A tiny white fleck sits in the dark eye of a painted bird
beats.summary: Gideon tells Ines about the tiny white fleck in the heron's eye, a slip of the brush he never dared to fix.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass held over the dark eye of a painted bird
beats.summary: Ines examines the eye of the hanging painting and finds no fleck at all.

beats.scene: Ines turns the painting and shows bright new tacks in the stretcher
beats.summary: The canvas is modern, the tacks are bright and the varnish smells fresh, so the painting is a copy.

beats.scene: Gideon shakes with anger while Dr Priya puts a hand on his arm
beats.summary: Gideon is wounded and furious that someone has copied his work and not even seen the fleck.

beats.scene: Ines stands in the middle of the study and thinks
beats.summary: Ines realises that the real Heron has been stolen and is worth a fortune.

beats.scene: A feather duster and a pail stand beside the study door
beats.summary: Mrs Bright says she dusted the study on Thursday, and the painting looked right to her then.

beats.scene: Mr Bell leans on the study door and scratches his chin
beats.summary: Mr Bell says that he heard someone in the study late on Thursday night and thought it was Orla.

beats.scene: Ines writes four names on a clean page and studies them
beats.summary: Ines sees that only the guests who slept at the lodge on Thursday could have changed the paintings.

beats.scene: Pale scrapes on the floor beneath the painting and a smear on the sash
beats.summary: Ines examines the floor and the window sash and finds scuffs and a smear of dark varnish.

beats.scene: Ines runs her fingers along the old wooden frame of the painting
beats.summary: She sees that the frame is the Heron's own, so the thief moved only the canvas.

beats.scene: An open visitors' book lies in the hall under a lamp
beats.summary: The visitors' book shows that Lucas viewed the Heron alone with Orla three weeks ago.

beats.scene: Lucas stands before the fire with one hand in his pocket
beats.summary: Lucas says that the painting was genuine when he valued it and a thief would need a forger and a week.

beats.scene: Felix leans against a bookcase and laughs, but not happily
beats.summary: Felix says he knows the house well, but he is no thief, and he has no one to sell to.

beats.scene: Tamsin hugs her notebook as she speaks to Ines in the hall
beats.summary: Tamsin admits she came because of a tip about copied paintings in houses valued by Reyes Fine Art.

beats.scene: A white cold store door and a row of hams in the kitchen
beats.summary: Mr Bell shows Ines the kitchen, the larder and the cold store where the meat is kept.

beats.scene: Mrs Bright wipes her hands on an apron and looks at the ceiling
beats.summary: Mrs Bright says Orla came up from the cellar at four o'clock on Friday looking pale and said nothing.

beats.scene: Ines sits alone with her notebook, tapping a pen on a page
beats.summary: Ines wonders what Orla found in the cellar at four, and what she meant to do about it.

beats.scene: Ines stands at the kitchen passage with a lantern, looking at the cellar door
beats.summary: Mrs Bright seems to want to say more, but Ines decides to look at the cellar by daylight.

beats.scene: Mrs Bright draws Ines into the pantry and speaks in a low voice
beats.summary: Mrs Bright says that Lucas came back from the kitchen passage, not from the cloakroom.

beats.scene: A clock on a kitchen wall shows two minutes to nine
beats.summary: Mrs Bright says that she heard the dull thump at two minutes to nine by the kitchen clock.

beats.scene: A dresser in the passage holds candles, matches and a lamp
beats.summary: Mrs Bright says that the only matches and candles near the passage are on her dresser, within an arm's reach of the cellar door.

beats.scene: Ines walks along a hall and a passage with her wristwatch held up
beats.summary: Ines times the walk from the table to the cloakroom and from the table to the cellar.

beats.scene: A row of candle holders in the hall, every one of them unlit
beats.summary: Ines checks the hall candle holders and finds them all unlit, so Lucas had not lit his candle in the hall.

beats.scene: Ines faces Lucas across a small table in the quiet lounge
beats.summary: Lucas says again that he only went to the cloakroom, but his story does not fit what Ines knows.

beats.scene: Lucas smiles and spreads his hands while Ines looks steadily at him
beats.summary: Lucas says that Mrs Bright was surely mistaken in the dark, and that nobody can prove anything.

beats.scene: Lucas stands at the door with his chin high
beats.summary: Lucas warns Ines that she is an insurance investigator, and that careless accusations can ruin a person.

beats.scene: A white streak of chalky dust on the cuff of a pale sleeve
beats.summary: After he leaves, Ines remembers a white streak on his cuff like the whitewash on the cellar wall.

beats.scene: Ines and Mr Bell stand at the top of the cellar steps with lanterns
beats.summary: Ines unlocks the cellar and goes down with Mr Bell in the daylight.

beats.scene: Stone steps lead down into a cold cellar lit by a lantern
beats.summary: In the cellar Ines sees the place where Orla fell, and chalk marks left by Dr Priya.

beats.scene: Rows of dusty bottles lie in racks along a whitewashed wall
beats.summary: Not one bottle has been taken from the racks, so Orla never reached the wine.

beats.scene: A white sheet is pulled back from a gilded frame in a corner
beats.summary: Behind the wine racks Ines finds an empty gold frame under a white sheet.

beats.scene: A paper label on the back of a gold frame
beats.summary: The frame carries a label from Reyes Fine Art, with a date from last week.

beats.scene: Ines measures the empty frame with a tape against her notes
beats.summary: The frame is exactly the size of The Grey Heron.

beats.scene: Ines stands in the cellar with the gold frame, thinking hard
beats.summary: Ines understands that the forgery was brought in this frame and hidden, and that Orla found it at four.

beats.scene: A pale line of whitewash rubbed from the wall near the steps
beats.summary: Ines finds fresh whitewash scraped off beside the steps, where someone brushed the wall in a struggle.

beats.scene: Mr Bell frowns as Ines explains, with his hand on the bolt
beats.summary: Ines tells Mr Bell that Orla came down to look at the frame again, met the thief and was pushed.

beats.scene: The sea beyond a window, with waves still high on the rocks
beats.summary: Mr Bell says that the real painting must still be on the island, since no one can leave.

beats.scene: Ines pulls a long list from her pocket and ticks the first line
beats.summary: Ines decides to search every room and every corner of the lodge, with the guests' consent.

beats.scene: A man's bedroom with clothes strewn across the bed and bills on a desk
beats.summary: In Felix's room Ines finds unpaid bills and a pawn ticket, but no painting.

beats.scene: An account book and a crumpled letter lie open on a small table
beats.summary: In Hugh's room Ines finds a ledger and a letter promising repayment, but no painting.

beats.scene: An old painter's room smelling of oil paint and tobacco
beats.summary: In Gideon's room Ines finds sketchbooks of the Heron, with the white fleck carefully marked.

beats.scene: A doctor's room with a neat bed and a worn leather bag
beats.summary: In Dr Priya's room Ines finds medicines and a letter from Orla, kind and private.

beats.scene: A lawyer's room with papers in neat piles
beats.summary: In Marta's room Ines finds files and a spare copy of the will, but no painting.

beats.scene: A journalist's room with a laptop, a notebook and a recorder
beats.summary: Tamsin will not open her notebook, but lets Ines hear her dinner recording: Lucas is silent, and a thump sounds at two minutes to nine.

beats.scene: A tidy room with one pale suit hanging beside a leather case
beats.summary: Lucas's room is too tidy, and the cuff of his pale suit is damp.

beats.scene: Lucas leans in the doorway of his room, smiling
beats.summary: Lucas stands in his doorway and thanks Ines politely for her trouble.

beats.scene: Mr Bell lifts the lid of a dusty chest in a cold attic
beats.summary: Mr Bell and Ines search the attic, the sheds, the boathouse and the jetty, and find nothing.

beats.scene: A young woman in a coat whispers to Ines in the hall at dusk
beats.summary: At dusk Tamsin whispers that she saw Lucas beside the hall clock very early on Saturday morning.

beats.scene: Tamsin sits on the stairs hugging her knees, speaking quietly
beats.summary: Tamsin says she was awake before dawn and saw Lucas open the little door of the clock.

beats.scene: Tamsin looks over her shoulder at the dark hall
beats.summary: Tamsin was afraid to speak earlier, because a man who steals paintings might be dangerous.

beats.scene: Ines puts a hand on Tamsin's arm on the stairs
beats.summary: Ines asks Tamsin to wait while she fetches Mr Bell and a lantern to open the clock together.

beats.scene: Tamsin tiptoes alone along the hall towards the tall clock
beats.summary: But Tamsin cannot wait, and she tiptoes alone towards the clock.

beats.scene: Felix and Gideon argue in the lounge while Hugh stands between them
beats.summary: Ines is called away to stop a quarrel between Felix and Gideon.

beats.scene: Ines stops in a quiet kitchen as a thumping noise begins
beats.summary: A faint banging from the kitchen sends Ines to look for Tamsin.

beats.scene: A white cold store door has a chair wedged under its handle
beats.summary: They follow the banging to the cold store, where the door is wedged shut with a chair.

beats.scene: Tamsin, shaking and wrapped in a blanket, sits by the kitchen stove
beats.summary: Tamsin is rescued and warmed, and Dr Priya sits with her.

beats.scene: Tamsin sips hot tea and describes a sleeve in the dark
beats.summary: Tamsin says she found a tube in the clock and then someone pushed her into the cold store, and she saw only a pale sleeve.

beats.scene: The case of the tall clock stands open with nothing inside
beats.summary: Ines opens the clock and finds that the tube has gone.

A1A2: Ines stood on the windy shore and looked at a small island far away.
Mr Bell, who looks after the island, drove up in an old car.
Mr Bell said the sea covers the stone road two times each day.
The old car drove across the road with the sea close on both sides.
Soon Ines saw Tern Rock Lodge, a grey stone house with tall chimneys.
Mr Bell showed her his blue boat, tied up beside the water.
Orla Venn stood at the door with her stick and smiled at Ines.
Orla took Ines into the hall, where a tall clock ticked loudly.
In the kitchen, Mrs Bright gave Ines hot tea and a big piece of cake.
Orla told Ines quietly that she was going to sell the lodge and its paintings.
Orla put her hand on the clock and said her husband wound it every Friday.
Orla opened the study door and showed Ines her best painting, The Grey Heron.
The painting showed a grey bird standing alone in the water at dawn.
In the lounge, Ines met Felix, Orla's nephew, who smiled a great deal.
Hugh Marlowe looked after Orla's money, and he spoke fast and looked worried.
Dr Priya Nair, Orla's doctor and good friend, spoke softly and listened well.
Gideon Frost was an old painter who had made The Grey Heron long ago.
Lucas Reyes, a man in a pale suit, sold paintings and smiled warmly.
Tamsin Reed wrote in a notebook, and Marta Okoye was Orla's careful lawyer.
Mr Bell looked out of the window and said a big storm was coming.
Mrs Bright took Ines up the stairs, past many pictures of the sea.
Ines put her bag down in a small room with a view of the sea.
Ines looked at the small old paintings on the landing and liked them.
One photograph showed Orla's husband, Captain Arthur Venn, with the men of the lifeboat.
Later, Ines went back to the study alone and looked closely at the painting.
The paint looked new and shiny, and it smelled fresh, which seemed strange.
Orla came in and asked Ines to look again in the morning.
Rain began to fall, and the wind shook the windows of the lodge.
Big waves rolled over the stone road, and Mr Bell said nobody could leave.
Then the telephone went dead, and no mobile phone had a signal.
At eight o'clock, the guests sat at a long table and ate hot soup.
Orla sat at the head of the table, and Ines sat near Gideon.
Hugh talked fast about money until Orla asked him kindly to stop.
Gideon said he hated modern paintings, and Lucas made a joke to calm him.
Orla stood up and told everyone that she was going to sell the lodge.
Felix was angry because he had always thought the lodge would be his.
Marta said nothing, and Dr Priya spoke kindly to calm the whole table.
At quarter to nine, Orla said she would get some special wine.
Orla took a key from the wall and walked into the dark passage.
A few minutes later, Lucas left the table to wash his hands.
The meat came, but Gideon said that Orla was taking a long time.
In the kitchen, Mrs Bright heard a heavy bump and thought it was the storm.
The clock struck nine, but Orla had still not come back.
Then, at five past nine, all the lights went out.
Lucas walked in with a candle and said he had been in the cloakroom.
Mr Bell looked at the electric box, but the storm had broken the line.
Ines asked where Orla was, but nobody had seen her for twenty minutes.
Ines and Mr Bell took candles and went along the dark passage.
The cellar door was closed, with an iron bolt across it on the outside.
Ines opened the door and saw Orla lying at the bottom of the steps.
Dr Priya bent down beside Orla, felt her wrist and said quietly that she was dead.
Orla's watch was broken, and it had stopped at two minutes to nine.
Dr Priya found a mark on Orla's shoulder, as if someone had pushed her hard.
Ines looked at the bolt and said that nobody could shut it from inside.
Ines found the key on the steps, so Orla had opened the door herself.
In the lounge, Ines told the guests that this was a crime.
Felix shouted and Gideon laughed, but Ines said she had worked for the police.
Mr Bell ran to the water and found his boat broken into pieces.
His radio was full of sea water, so nobody could call for help.
Ines covered Orla with a blanket, shut the door and kept the key.
Ines asked everyone where they were at two minutes to nine.
Hugh, Gideon, Tamsin, Marta and Dr Priya all said they were at the table.
Lucas said he had been in the cloakroom, but nobody had seen him there.
The cloakroom was at the front, and the cellar was at the back.
Ines wrote down every name and asked who would be better off without Orla.
Mr Bell and Ines checked every door and window, and all of them were locked.
Nobody ate much supper, so Ines told everyone to lock their doors.
In her room, Ines thought about the bolt and the person who shut it.
At midnight, Ines heard a soft sound downstairs and went to look.
In the study, Ines found Felix opening drawers, and he ran away.
Saturday came grey and wet, and the guests ate breakfast in silence.
Felix said he had been looking for the new will in the study.
He owed a lot of money, and Orla had refused to help him.
Ines thought Felix wanted money, but he also needed his aunt to be alive.
Marta told Ines that Orla's new will gave the lodge to the lifeboat.
Orla had signed it two weeks ago and planned to tell Felix kindly.
Dr Priya said that Orla's heart was weak, so she had little time left.
Hugh said he had taken money from Orla's account, but he was at dinner.
Mrs Bright said Hugh never left his chair all evening.
Ines remembered Orla's words about the morning light and went into the study.
Ines asked Gideon to look at the painting, and he stared at it.
Gideon sat down and said he painted the heron forty years ago.
He told Ines about a tiny white mark in the eye of the bird.
Ines held her glass over the bird's eye, but she saw no white mark.
The canvas was new, and the nails were bright, so the painting was a copy.
Gideon was shaking with anger, and Dr Priya put a hand on his arm.
Ines understood that someone had stolen the real painting, which was worth a fortune.
Mrs Bright said she cleaned the study on Thursday, and the painting looked right.
Mr Bell said he heard someone in the study late on Thursday night.
Only the people at the lodge on Thursday night could have changed the paintings.
Ines looked at the floor and the window and found marks on both.
The frame was the old one, so the thief had only moved the canvas.
The visitors' book showed that Lucas came three weeks ago and measured the painting.
Lucas said the painting was real when he saw it, and he smiled.
Felix said he knew the house, but he was no thief.
Tamsin said she came because of a story about copied paintings in other houses.
Mr Bell showed Ines the big kitchen and the cold store.
Mrs Bright said Orla came up from the cellar at four, looking pale.
Ines wondered what Orla had seen in the cellar, and what she planned to do.
Mrs Bright seemed to want to say more, but Ines went to the cellar.
Mrs Bright told Ines that Lucas came from the back passage, not the cloakroom.
She also heard a heavy bump at two minutes to nine by the kitchen clock.
The only candles and matches near the cellar were on her own dresser.
Ines walked from the table to the cloakroom and to the cellar, timing each one.
Ines checked the hall and found that no candle had been used.
Ines sat opposite Lucas, and he said again that he went to the cloakroom.
Lucas smiled and said Mrs Bright was wrong, and nobody could prove it.
He warned Ines that careless words could ruin a person.
After he left, Ines remembered a white mark on his sleeve, like the cellar wall.
Ines unlocked the cellar, and she and Mr Bell went down in the daylight.
In the daylight, the cellar looked cold and plain, and Ines looked at every corner.
Not one bottle was missing from the racks, so Orla never reached the wine.
Behind the racks, Ines found a gold frame under a white sheet.
On the back of the frame was a label from Reyes Fine Art.
The frame was exactly the same size as The Grey Heron.
Ines understood that the copy had come in this frame, and Orla had found it.
Near the steps, a part of the white wall had been rubbed away.
Ines told Mr Bell that Orla came to see the frame, and someone pushed her.
Mr Bell said the real painting must still be on the island.
Ines decided to search every room in the lodge, with everyone's permission.
In Felix's room, Ines found many bills, but no painting.
In Hugh's room, there was a book of accounts and a letter, but no painting.
In Gideon's room, she found drawings of the heron with the white mark.
In Dr Priya's room, there were medicines and a kind letter from Orla.
Marta's room held neat files and a copy of the will, but no painting.
Tamsin let Ines hear her recording, and Lucas's voice was missing for a while.
Lucas's room was very tidy, and his pale suit hung wet at the sleeve.
Lucas stood in his doorway, smiling, and thanked Ines for her trouble.
They also searched the attic, the sheds and the boathouse, but found nothing.
At dusk, Tamsin whispered that she saw Lucas beside the hall clock early that morning.
Before dawn, Tamsin saw Lucas open the small door of the clock.
She was afraid to tell anyone, because she thought Lucas could be dangerous.
Ines told her to wait while she fetched Mr Bell and a lantern.
But Tamsin could not wait, and she walked alone towards the clock.
Meanwhile, Felix and Gideon began a loud quarrel, and Ines had to stop it.
Then Ines heard a faint banging from the kitchen and went to look.
The banging came from the cold store, where a chair held the door shut.
They opened the door, and Tamsin came out, shaking and very cold.
Tamsin said she found a tube in the clock, and then someone pushed her.
Ines opened the clock, but the tube was gone.
For ten minutes, everyone had a witness, but nobody could say where Lucas was.
Ines read the tide table, and the sea road would open at twenty to five.
Mr Bell tapped the glass in the hall and said the storm was getting weaker.
Ines thought that Lucas had hidden the tube outside and would come for it.
Ines told Mr Bell, Felix and Dr Priya her plan, and they agreed to help.
Felix stood up straight and asked to have a part in the plan.
Ines asked Mrs Bright to leave the back door open and the kitchen dark.
At supper, Ines said that Mr Bell would fetch the police at dawn.
She said that every bag would be searched, and Lucas's finger tapped his cup.
Dr Priya took Tamsin upstairs to her room, and the plan was ready.
The guests sat by the fire, and Lucas talked politely about the weather.
Gideon told a story about Orla and Arthur and how they bought the heron.
Marta said Orla chose the lifeboat because the crew had carried Arthur's coffin.
Hugh told Ines that he would write the whole truth and repay every penny.
By midnight, the rain had stopped, and the wind began to fall.
The guests went up to bed, and Lucas said goodnight and went to his room.
Ines sat in the dark kitchen and listened as the clock struck twelve.
Mrs Bright left some tea for Ines and went to bed, and one o'clock struck.
Mr Bell and Felix hid beside the back path with a covered lantern.
Ines waited as two o'clock struck and the wind died away.
At three in the morning, Ines heard someone coming down the stairs.
Lucas walked through the kitchen in a long coat and went out the back door.
Ines followed him quietly, and Mr Bell joined her while Felix ran ahead.
Lucas took a rocky path to the shore with a small torch.
Ines and Mr Bell followed him to the boathouse and stopped at the door.
Inside, Lucas reached into the broken boat and took out a long tube.
Ines whispered that they must wait, because the water in the boathouse was deep.
Lucas came out with the tube and walked towards the sea road.
The storm was over, and the stone road began to show above the water.
Lucas stood at the edge of the water and looked at his watch.
The sea went down slowly, and the wet stones of the road appeared.
Lucas stepped onto the road and walked fast, holding the tube tightly.
Ines stepped onto the road behind him with a lantern and called his name.
Lucas turned, saw the light and knew that he was trapped.
He began to run, but Felix and Mr Bell ran after him.
They raced over the slippery stones with the sea on both sides.
Lucas tried to throw the tube into the sea, but Felix pulled it away.
Then Lucas slipped on the weed and fell, and Mr Bell held him down.
Lucas stopped fighting and sat on a flat stone with his head down.
Grey morning light spread over the sea, and the road looked wide and pale.
Mr Bell hurried across the road to fetch the police, and Ines guarded Lucas.
Lucas said he stole the painting because he owed too much money.
On Thursday night he changed the paintings and hid the gold frame.
Orla found the frame and told him she would tell the police.
He pushed her, she fell, and he shut the bolt and took a candle.
Lucas said he was sorry that he had locked Tamsin in the cold store.
Ines opened the tube and took out the real Grey Heron.
In the bird's eye, there was the tiny white mark.
Ines told Felix how the bolt, the watch and the candle had caught Lucas.
The police came across the sea road at sunrise and took Lucas away.
One officer took Lucas away, and the other came up to the lodge.
In the lounge, Ines told the police everything and gave them her notebook.
At breakfast, Hugh promised to repay every penny he had borrowed.
Felix said he was ashamed, and he would work to pay his debts.
Gideon saw the real heron again, laughed at the little mark and cried.
Tamsin said she would write the true story and thanked Ines.
Mrs Bright poured the tea, and Mr Bell talked about a new boat.
Marta told everyone that the lodge would go to the lifeboat, as Orla wished.
In the quiet study, Ines said goodbye to Orla and the old clock.
Ines left the island; the lodge would help people who save lives at sea.
B1B2: Ines Calloway reaches the shore on Friday afternoon, with one suitcase and a notebook full of questions. Across a mile of shining sand lies Tern Rock, a dark island under a heavy sky.

A battered car rattles up beside her, and a broad man in a waxed coat leans out of the window. He introduces himself as Mr Bell, the caretaker and boatman, and says he has come to carry her across before the tide turns.

Mr Bell points to tall white posts standing in the sand and explains that the sea covers the road twice every day. If the water reaches the third post, he says, nobody crosses until the tide has fallen again.
The car bumps over the wet stones, with small waves lapping close on either side. Ahead of them, a bank of dark cloud is rising slowly above the sea.
At the end of the causeway the island rises, and Tern Rock Lodge stands on its highest point. It is an old grey house with tall chimneys, small windows and a roof streaked with salt.

Below the lodge, a stone jetty reaches into a small harbour where the gulls are crying. Mr Bell shows her his blue boat and the boathouse, which are the island's only way off when the sea road is closed.
Orla Venn is waiting at the lodge door, leaning on a silver-topped stick. She is small and upright, and although she is seventy years old, her eyes are bright and quick.
Orla leads Ines into a wide hall where a tall clock is ticking and voices drift from the lounge. The other guests have all arrived, she says, and Ines will meet them soon.
In the warm kitchen, Mrs Bright pours Ines a cup of strong tea and cuts her a slice of fruitcake. The larder is full, she says, in case the storm keeps everybody indoors.

Orla draws Ines into a quiet corner and says quietly that she is going to sell the lodge and every painting in it. She wants Ines, as an insurance investigator, to examine the pictures carefully and to tell her the truth.
Orla rests her hand on the case of the tall grandfather clock. Her late husband wound it every Friday, she says, and since his death she has done it herself.
The study is a small room lined with books, and a large painting hangs above the fireplace. Orla says it is the best thing she owns, and she calls it The Grey Heron.
The painting shows a lone grey bird standing in shallow water at dawn. Orla says it is worth more than the whole island and every stone on it.
In the lounge, a handsome man rises from a chair beside the log fire. This is Felix, Orla's nephew, who greets Ines warmly although he looks tired around the eyes.
Hugh Marlowe, who looks after Orla's accounts, shakes hands with damp fingers. He talks so quickly about the sale that Ines can hardly follow him.
Dr Priya Nair is Orla's doctor and her oldest friend, and she smiles calmly at Ines. She speaks softly, but Ines notices that she watches everyone in the room.
Gideon Frost is an old painter with paint-stained fingers and a very bad temper. He painted The Grey Heron many years ago, and he does not like to talk about it.
Lucas Reyes wears a pale suit and shakes Ines's hand with a charming smile. He is an art dealer who acts for the buyer of the lodge.

A young woman called Tamsin Reed sits writing in a notebook beside the window, and she says she is a journalist. Next to her sits Marta Okoye, Orla's lawyer, who watches Ines carefully and says very little.
Mr Bell comes in from the garden, holding his cap against the rising wind. He says that a storm is coming, and that the sea road will close tonight.

Mrs Bright shows Ines up the wide staircase, where the walls are crowded with paintings of the sea. There are ships, harbours and storms in tarnished gold frames, and she says that Captain Venn bought most of them.

Ines's room is small and plain, with a narrow bed and a window that looks over the jetty and the sea road. She unpacks her notebook, a small magnifying glass and her torch, and puts the torch beside the bed.

On the landing hang a dozen small oil paintings, old and dusty, which have never been valued. Ines examines each one with her glass and decides that they are honest pictures, worth little money and a great deal of care.

Beside the window hangs a photograph of men in oilskins standing in front of a lifeboat. A brass plate names the tall man in the middle as Captain Arthur Venn, Orla's husband, who led the lifeboat crew for thirty years.
Before dinner Ines slips back into the study alone and lights the lamp. She stands in front of The Grey Heron, and for a long moment she cannot say why it troubles her.
Then she notices that the varnish shines brightly, and when she leans close she can smell it. She tells herself that she is no expert, but old paintings do not usually smell new.
Orla comes in, tapping her stick on the floor, and asks what Ines thinks of the Heron. Before Ines can answer, she says lightly that it would be better to look again tomorrow in daylight.
By six o'clock the wind has become a roar, and the first heavy drops of rain strike the windows. The guests gather in the lounge as the light fades, and Mrs Bright goes round lighting the lamps.
From the lounge window Ines watches the waves climb the causeway until the road has vanished beneath the sea. Mr Bell says that nobody will cross it tonight, and perhaps not before Sunday.
In the hall, Felix lifts the telephone and then puts it down again with a puzzled frown. The line is dead, and when the guests check their mobile phones, none of them can find a signal.
At eight o'clock the guests sit down at a long table laid with silver and candles. Mrs Bright carries in bowls of hot soup, and Mr Bell stands ready to pour the wine.
Orla sits at the head of the table with Marta on her right, and Ines is placed between Gideon and Dr Priya. Felix sits opposite Ines, and Lucas, Hugh and Tamsin fill the remaining places.
Hugh talks fast about figures and taxes, and his soup grows cold in front of him. At last Orla touches his hand and asks him, very kindly, to let the soup be eaten first.
Gideon complains loudly that modern painters cannot draw a bird or a boat, and the table goes quiet. Lucas makes a smooth joke to calm him, while Tamsin asks questions that nobody wants to answer.

Between the soup and the main course, Orla rises with a glass in her hand and asks for silence. She announces that she has decided to sell the lodge to a buyer from abroad, and that Lucas will arrange everything.
Felix puts down his spoon so hard that it rings against the plate. He has always believed that the lodge would be his, and he stares at his aunt with open anger.
Marta rests her hand on a folder and says nothing, but Ines sees her eyes flick towards Felix. Dr Priya speaks calmly to quiet the table, and Orla promises Felix a private talk after dinner.

The clock in the hall strikes the quarter, and Orla says that this evening deserves a very special bottle of wine. She has kept it in the cellar for years, she says, and tonight she will fetch it herself.
Orla takes a heavy key from its hook beside the door at the back of the room. Her stick taps slowly away along the stone passage, and then the sound is lost in the noise of the wind.
A few minutes later Lucas pushes back his chair and says that he must wash his hands. Hugh goes on talking about money, and Mrs Bright sets the main course on the table.
The roast lamb is served, but the guests eat little, and Orla's chair stays empty. Gideon grumbles that a bottle of wine should not take so long to find.

In the kitchen, Mrs Bright is lifting a dish from the stove when she hears a dull thump from the back passage. She glances at the kitchen clock, which shows two minutes to nine, and decides that it was only the storm.
In the hall the clock strikes nine, and still there is no sign of Orla. Dr Priya glances at the door more than once, and Ines sees that her calm is beginning to crack.
At five past nine, every light in the lodge goes out at the same moment, and the room is black. Someone cries out, a glass falls over, and the wind sounds suddenly very loud.
A moment later a candle flame appears in the doorway from the hall, and Lucas steps into the room. He says that he has been in the cloakroom, and that he found a candle on his way back.
Mr Bell fetches a lamp from the kitchen and checks the fuse box in the hall. Everything is in order, so the storm must have broken the power line from the mainland.
Ines looks at Orla's empty chair and asks where she is. Nobody has seen her since a quarter to nine, and that was twenty minutes ago.
Ines takes a candle, and Mr Bell takes the lamp, and together they walk into the long passage behind the kitchen. The stone walls are cold and wet, and the flames shake in the draught.
At the end of the passage they reach the cellar door, which is closed. An iron bolt on the outside has been pushed firmly across.
Ines draws back the bolt and opens the door, and the lamplight falls on the steps below. At the bottom, Orla Venn is lying very still.
Dr Priya kneels beside Orla, feels her wrist and looks up with a grave face. She says quietly that Orla is dead, and that she cannot have lived for long after the fall.
Ines holds her candle close to Orla's thin wrist, where a small gold watch lies cracked. The hands have stopped at two minutes to nine, so that must be the moment when Orla fell.
Dr Priya says that the fall killed Orla, but she points to a dark bruise on her shoulder. She is not a police doctor, she adds, but it looks to her like the mark of a hard shove.
Ines goes back up the steps and studies the iron bolt on the outer face of the door. Nobody can bolt a door from the wrong side, she says, so this was no accident.
On the second step Ines finds a heavy iron key, lying where it fell from Orla's hand. This means that Orla opened the lock herself, and that someone else shot the bolt behind her.
Ines asks the guests to come to the lounge, and she shuts the door behind them. She tells them that Orla did not die by accident, and that she must treat the matter as a crime.
Felix shouts that she has no right, and Gideon snorts that an insurance woman is not a detective. Ines explains calmly that she served six years in the police, and the room falls silent.
Mr Bell puts on his coat and goes out to check the boat, in spite of the storm. He returns half an hour later, soaked and grim, and says that the waves have smashed it to pieces.
He has also tried the radio that he keeps in the boathouse, but sea water has ruined it. Without a boat or a radio, there is no way to call for help.
Ines covers Orla gently with a blanket from the kitchen and locks the cellar door. She puts the heavy key in her pocket and asks everyone to stay together.
Ines gathers the guests in the lounge and asks each one where they were at two minutes to nine. She writes down every answer in her notebook, and she watches every face while they speak.
Hugh, Gideon, Tamsin, Marta and Dr Priya all say that they were sitting at the dinner table. Mr Bell says that he was pouring wine in the same room, and Felix says that he was staring at his plate.
Lucas says that he was in the cloakroom at that time, and that the lights went out while he was washing his hands. Everyone remembers that he left the table, but nobody saw where he went.

On a page of her notebook Ines draws a plan of the lodge, and she sees that the cloakroom is at the front. The cellar is at the back, past the kitchen, and the two are as far apart as any two rooms can be.

Ines writes down three names: Felix, who expected to inherit; Hugh, whose accounts would be examined; and Lucas, who left the table. She puts a question mark beside each of them, and then sits looking at the page for a long time.
Mr Bell and Ines walk through the lodge with a lantern, trying every door and window. All of them are locked from the inside, so no stranger has come in from the storm.
In the lounge a cold supper is laid out, but nobody has any appetite. Ines asks everyone to lock their bedroom doors and not to wander about the house alone.
Alone in her room, Ines sits on the edge of the bed and thinks about the bolt. Orla was small and light, so the killer did not need to be strong, and that makes the list of suspects longer.
At midnight Ines hears a floorboard creak somewhere below her. She takes her torch, opens her door very quietly and creeps down the stairs.

Her torch beam finds the study door standing open, and a man kneeling beside the desk with a drawer in his hands. It is Felix, and as soon as the light touches his face, he drops the drawer and runs out into the dark.
Saturday dawns grey and wet, with rain still streaming down the windows. The guests come down to a silent breakfast, and nobody looks at anybody else.
Felix is sitting alone in the lounge with his head in his hands when Ines finds him. He admits that he was searching the study for his aunt's new will, because he wanted to know what she had decided.
He owes a large sum to a man who does not forgive late payments, he says. A month ago he asked his aunt for help, but she refused, and he has hardly slept since.
Ines weighs what she has heard, and she sees that Felix had a motive. But he also needed his aunt alive until she changed her mind, so it is not as simple as it looks.
In the library Marta Okoye opens her leather folder and takes out a folded paper. The new will, she says, leaves the lodge to the Tern Rock Lifeboat, and gives Felix only a small sum and a letter.
Orla signed the will two weeks ago, Marta explains, and she meant to tell Felix gently after dinner. She also meant the toast to be for the lifeboat, but she never had the chance to say so.

Dr Priya sits by the window with her bag on her knees and says that Orla had a weak heart. She had perhaps a year to live, the doctor says, and that is why Orla wanted to sell the lodge and put everything in order.

When Ines asks to see the accounts, Hugh Marlowe turns the colour of paper and admits that he has been borrowing from Orla's money. He swears that he meant to repay every penny, and that he was at the dinner table all evening.
Mrs Bright, who is scrubbing a pan in the kitchen, says that Hugh never left his chair all evening. She was in and out with dishes, she says, and each time she came in he was talking.
Ines remembers that Orla asked her to look at the Heron again in daylight. She stands alone at the study door for a moment, and then she goes in.

Ines asks Gideon to come into the study, and she opens the curtains to let in the grey morning light. The old man stares at The Grey Heron, nose almost touching the canvas, and then he says that it is not his.
Gideon sinks into a chair and says that he painted the Heron forty years ago, in a rented room by the sea. He worked on it for a whole winter, and Orla bought it at his first exhibition.
Every painter leaves a mark, Gideon says, and his was a tiny white fleck in the heron's eye. It was a slip of the brush, but it made the eye look alive, so he never painted it out.
Ines takes out her magnifying glass and holds it over the dark eye of the bird. She searches every corner of it, but there is no white fleck at all.
Together they lift the painting off its hook and look at the back of the canvas. The tacks are bright and new, the wood is pale, and the varnish smells fresh, so this painting is a copy.
Gideon shakes with anger, because someone has copied his work and has not even noticed the fleck. Dr Priya, who has come in quietly, puts a hand on his arm and leads him to a chair.
Ines stands in the middle of the study and understands what this means. The real Grey Heron has been stolen, and a painting worth a fortune has been replaced by a clever fake.
Mrs Bright says that she dusted the study on Thursday morning and that the painting looked just as always. If it was changed, she says, it was changed after that.
Mr Bell leans in the study doorway and scratches his chin. He says that he heard someone moving in the study late on Thursday night, and that he thought it was Orla.
Ines writes four names on a page and looks at them for a long time. Only the guests who slept at the lodge on Thursday night could have changed the paintings: Felix, Hugh, Gideon and Lucas.

Ines kneels in front of the painting and finds pale scrapes on the floor where a ladder has stood. On the window sash there is a smear of varnish, as if someone opened the window to blow away the smell.

She runs her fingers along the old wooden frame and sees that it is the Heron's own, with no new marks. The thief has taken only the canvas, which means that he worked quickly and knew what he was doing.
The visitors' book in the hall lists everyone who has come to the lodge this month. Three weeks ago Lucas Reyes spent an afternoon in the study, measuring the Heron for the buyer.
Lucas stands by the fire with one hand in his pocket and says that the painting was genuine when he saw it. A thief, he adds with a smile, would need a skilful forger and at least a week.
Felix leans against a bookcase and laughs, but not happily. He says that he knows the house well, but he is no thief, and he would not know whom to sell a painting to.
Tamsin hugs her notebook and speaks quietly to Ines in the hall. She admits that she came because of a tip about copied paintings in houses that were valued by Reyes Fine Art.
Mr Bell takes Ines through the kitchen, the larder and the cold store, where hams hang from hooks. The cold store has a heavy white door with a handle on the outside only.
Mrs Bright wipes her hands on her apron and says that Orla came up from the cellar at four o'clock on Friday. She looked pale, the cook says, and she said nothing to anyone.
Ines sits alone with her notebook and taps her pen on the page. She wonders what Orla found in the cellar at four, and what she meant to do about it.
Mrs Bright seems to want to say more, but she says nothing in front of the others. Ines takes a lantern to the end of the kitchen passage and decides to examine the cellar properly in daylight.
Mrs Bright draws Ines into the pantry and closes the door. She says in a low voice that Lucas came back from the kitchen passage, not from the cloakroom.
Mrs Bright also says that she heard a heavy bump from the passage at two minutes to nine, by the kitchen clock. She thought it was the storm, she says, and she has been sorry ever since.

The only candles and matches near the cellar are on the dresser in the passage, within an arm's reach of the cellar door. When the lights failed, she says, she saw a man come out of the passage with a candle already lit.
Ines walks from the dining room to the cloakroom and back, with her wristwatch held up. Then she walks to the cellar door and back, and finds that either trip takes about two minutes.
She goes round the hall and checks every candle holder, and every one is cold and unlit. There is no candle on the hall table either, so Lucas did not find one there.
Ines sits across a small table from Lucas in the quiet lounge. He tells her again that he was in the cloakroom, and that he picked up a candle from the hall table.

Ines tells him that the hall table holds no candle, and that Mrs Bright saw him come out of the passage. Lucas spreads his hands and says that the cook was mistaken in the dark, and that nobody can prove anything.
Lucas stands up and warns Ines that she is only an insurance investigator. Careless accusations, he says in a soft voice, can ruin a person for ever.
When he has gone, Ines remembers a white streak of dust on his cuff when he came in with the candle. It looked very much like the whitewash on the cellar walls.
Ines unlocks the cellar door with the heavy key and goes down the steps with Mr Bell. A little grey daylight comes in through a grating high in the back wall, and they carry lanterns as well.
In the grey light from the grating the cellar looks small and cold. The blanket lies at the foot of the steps, and Ines pauses for a moment before she goes on.
Rows of dusty bottles lie in racks along the whitewashed walls, and the dust on every one is undisturbed. Not a single bottle has been taken out, so Orla never reached the wine she had come for.
Behind the last rack, in the darkest corner, Ines finds a large shape under a white sheet. She pulls the sheet back and uncovers an empty gold frame.
A paper label is stuck to the back of the frame. It says Reyes Fine Art, with a number and a date from last week.
Ines takes her tape measure from her pocket and measures the frame carefully. It is exactly the same size as the frame of The Grey Heron in the study.
Ines stands in the cellar and works it out slowly. The forged painting arrived in this gold frame, and the thief hid the frame down here, where Orla found it at four o'clock on Friday.
Near the foot of the steps a patch of whitewash has been scraped from the wall. The scrape is at the height of a man's shoulder, and the white dust beneath it is fresh.
Ines explains to Mr Bell what she believes happened on Friday evening. Orla came down again that evening to look at the frame, the thief followed her, and in a quarrel on the steps he pushed her.
Mr Bell frowns and looks up at the grating, where the grey sky shows. He says that the real painting cannot have left the island, because nobody could cross the sea.
Ines takes a list from her pocket and puts a tick beside the first line. She will search every room and every corner of the lodge, with the guests' permission.
In Felix's room Ines finds a pile of unpaid bills and a pawn ticket for a gold watch. There is no painting in the cupboard, under the bed or behind the curtains.
Hugh's room contains a neat account book and an unfinished letter to Orla, promising to repay every penny. There is no painting there, only a nervous man's list of what he owes.

Gideon's room smells of oil paint and tobacco, and his sketchbooks lie open on the bed. They are full of drawings of the Heron, and in each one the tiny white fleck in the eye is marked with a circle.
Dr Priya's room is tidy, with a row of medicine bottles beside a worn leather bag. She shows Ines a letter from Orla, kind and private, which thanks her for always telling the truth.
In Marta's room Ines finds neat piles of papers and a spare copy of the new will. Marta watches from the doorway with folded arms, and says that she has nothing to hide.

Tamsin refuses to open her notebook, but she lets Ines listen to the small recorder that she ran during dinner. On the recording, Lucas is silent from ten to nine until the lights fail, and a faint thump sounds at two minutes to nine.
Lucas's room is almost too tidy, with every shirt folded and every shoe in a line. His pale suit hangs on a hook, and its right sleeve is damp, as if someone has sponged it.
Lucas leans in the doorway of his room, smiling pleasantly. He thanks Ines for her trouble and says that he hopes she has found everything she wanted.
Mr Bell and Ines search the attic, the garden sheds, the boathouse and the end of the jetty. They find nothing but old trunks, nets, broken chairs and the ruins of Mr Bell's boat.
At dusk Tamsin catches Ines in the hall and whispers in her ear. She says that very early that morning, before it was light, she saw Lucas standing beside the tall clock.
Tamsin sits on the stairs hugging her knees and speaks very quietly. She woke before dawn and went down to write, she says, and she saw Lucas open the little door of the clock.
She did not tell Ines earlier, she says, because she was afraid of him. A man who could steal a painting, she thinks, might do something worse to a journalist who asks questions.
Ines takes her arm and tells her to wait. She will fetch Mr Bell and a lantern, she says, and they will open the clock together.
But Tamsin has never been good at waiting for other people to act. As soon as Ines has gone, she tiptoes along the dark hall towards the tall clock.
On her way to find Mr Bell, Ines hears Felix and Gideon quarrelling loudly in the lounge, while Hugh tries to stand between them. It takes her ten minutes to calm them down.
As the quarrel ends, Ines hears a faint banging somewhere in the kitchen. She looks for Tamsin in the hall, finds nobody and follows the noise.
The banging leads them to the cold store, where a chair has been wedged under the door handle. Mr Bell pulls the chair away and swings the heavy door open.
Tamsin stumbles out into the kitchen, shaking with fear and cold. Dr Priya wraps a blanket around her and sits her down by the warm kitchen stove.
When she can speak, Tamsin says that she opened the clock and found a long tube inside. Somebody seized her from behind and pushed her into the cold store, and all she saw was a pale sleeve.
Ines opens the little door in the clock case and looks inside. There is nothing there at all, and the tube has gone.
Ines asks everyone where they were during the ten minutes of the quarrel. Felix, Gideon, Hugh, Marta and Dr Priya each have a witness, but Lucas says only that he was walking alone.
Ines studies the printed table of tides beside a candle in the hall. It shows that the sea road will be clear of water at twenty to five on Sunday morning.
Mr Bell taps the barometer on the wall and nods slowly. The storm is easing, he says, and the sea road should open on time.
Ines spreads a map of the island on the kitchen table and thinks aloud. The tube is no longer in the lodge, she says, so Lucas has hidden it outside, where he can fetch it before he leaves.

Lucas cannot leave until the sea road opens, Ines explains, and he will want to be gone before the police arrive. She tells Mr Bell, Felix and Dr Priya her plan in a low voice, and they agree to help.
Felix straightens his back and says that he wants to make up for his foolishness. Ines shakes his hand and gives him a place beside Mr Bell.
Ines whispers to Mrs Bright by the stove and asks her to leave the back door unbolted. The cook nods, and promises to keep the kitchen dark tonight.

At supper in the lounge, Ines announces that Mr Bell will cross the sea road at first light and fetch the police. Nobody will be allowed to leave the island, she adds, until every bag has been searched.
Lucas lifts his cup of tea but does not drink it. His finger taps the rim, once and then again, and Ines pretends not to see.
Dr Priya takes Tamsin upstairs to her own room and locks the door. Everything is ready, and now there is nothing to do but wait.
The guests sit around the lounge fire, listening to the clock in the hall. Lucas chats politely about the weather, as if nothing in the world were wrong.

Gideon stares into the flames and tells a story about Orla and her husband. Long ago, he says, they bought the Heron for almost nothing from a very poor young painter, and they hung it over their first fire.
Marta says that Orla chose the lifeboat because its crew carried her husband's coffin ten years ago. Every Christmas since then, she says, the crew has brought Orla a basket of fish.
Hugh sits very straight and writes quickly on a sheet of paper. He tells Ines that he will give the buyer's lawyers a full confession, and that he will repay every penny.
By midnight the rain has stopped, and the wind begins to fall. The sound of the sea changes from a roar to a long, deep sigh.
One by one the guests go up to bed with their candles. Lucas yawns, says goodnight in his smooth voice, and walks slowly to his room.
Ines sits in the dark kitchen beside the window, with her notebook shut on her knee. In the hall the clock strikes midnight, and she listens to the echo fade.
Mrs Bright leaves a flask of hot tea and a currant bun on the table and goes to bed. The clock strikes one, and nothing has moved in the lodge.
Outside, Mr Bell and Felix crouch beside the back path under an old tarpaulin. They have a lantern with a cloth over it, and they are both shivering.
At two o'clock the clock strikes again, and Ines hears the last of the wind die away. Through the window she sees a few stars between the clouds.
At three o'clock in the morning, a stair creaks in the dark lodge. Ines holds her breath as someone begins to come down, very slowly and very carefully.
A figure in a long coat tiptoes into the dark kitchen, and Ines, in her corner, hardly breathes. It is Lucas, and he opens the back door without a sound and slips out into the night.
Ines slips off her shoes and follows him out into the cold air. Mr Bell rises from under his tarpaulin and joins her, while Felix runs ahead along the shore.
Lucas follows the narrow path among the black rocks, with a small torch that he keeps pointed at the ground. Overhead, a few faint stars shine through the broken clouds.
The path leads to the boathouse, a dark stone building at the water's edge. Ines and Mr Bell creep along the wall and stop beside the open door.
Inside, a thin beam of light moves over the ruined boat. Lucas reaches under the broken seat and pulls out a long cardboard tube.
Mr Bell raises a fist to rush in, but Ines catches his arm and whispers a warning. The water under the boathouse floor is deep and black, and she wants Lucas out on the shallows.
Lucas tucks the tube under his arm and walks out of the boathouse towards the shore. He does not look behind him, and the two shadows behind him stay perfectly still.
The storm has passed, and the first stones of the sea road are beginning to show above the water. In the starlight the causeway looks like a pale ribbon laid across the black sea.
Lucas stops at the edge of the sea and looks at his watch by the light of his torch. He is waiting for the tide to fall, and Ines is waiting for him.
The sea falls slowly, and the black stones of the causeway appear one by one. The white tide posts stand up from the water like the masts of a drowned ship.
Lucas steps onto the wet causeway with the tube clutched tightly against his chest. He walks fast, and the water sucks at his shoes.
Ines steps onto the road behind him, holding the lantern high. She calls his name, and her voice carries clearly over the water.
Lucas turns round and stares into the glare of the lantern. For a moment he stands quite still, and Ines can see that he understands everything.
Then he begins to run, with the tube under his arm. But Felix springs out of the rocks, and Mr Bell rushes after him along the road.
The chase goes along the slippery stones, with the sea on both sides. Lucas is fast, but the wet weed makes every step dangerous.
Lucas swings the tube back to throw it into the sea. Felix leaps forward with a cry and tears it from his hands at the very moment of the throw.
Lucas tries to run on, but he slips on the weed and falls hard on the stones. Mr Bell is on him at once, and holds him down.
Lucas does not struggle any more, and he lets Mr Bell help him up. He sits on a flat stone with his head bowed, and the fight has gone out of him.
The first grey light of dawn spreads over the sea and the long wet road. In the east, behind the clouds, the sky is slowly turning pale.
Mr Bell hurries away along the causeway to fetch the police, his boots splashing on the wet stones. Ines and Felix stay behind to guard Lucas, who sits very still.
Lucas speaks quietly, without once looking up at the others. He says that he stole the painting because he owed more money than he could ever repay.

On Thursday night, he says, he lifted the real Heron from its frame and hung a copy in its place. A forger in the city had painted the copy, and it had arrived in a gold frame, which he hid in the cellar.

On Friday afternoon Orla found the empty gold frame, and at dinner he saw by her face that she knew. When she went down to the cellar, he followed her, and at the cellar door she told him that she would call the police.
He pushed her, he says, and she fell down the steps and did not move. In a panic he bolted the door, and later he took a candle from the dresser and went back to the table.
Lucas says that he is sorry about Tamsin, and that he only wanted time to move the tube. He swears that he never meant to hurt anyone, but Ines tells him that Orla is dead.
In the grey light Ines kneels on the road and opens the end of the tube with care. She draws out a roll of canvas and unrolls it a little way, and there is the real Grey Heron.
The bird stands in the pale water, with its long neck folded. In its dark eye, tiny and perfect, there is a fleck of white.
Felix asks Ines how she knew, and she counts the clues on her fingers. The bolt proved it was murder, the stopped watch gave her the time, and the candle and the whitewash put Lucas in the passage.
At sunrise two police officers in yellow coats walk across the causeway, with Mr Bell beside them. They listen to Ines, take the tube and arrest Lucas Reyes.
One of the officers leads Lucas away to the police car, which is waiting on the far shore. The other walks up to the lodge with Ines and Felix to take their statements.
In the lounge Ines tells the officer everything, from the cellar bolt to the tube in the boathouse. She hands over her notebook, and he reads it with growing respect.
At breakfast the long table is bright with sunshine, and the guests eat hungrily at last. Hugh stands up and promises, with a shaking voice, to repay every penny he has borrowed.
Felix stands in front of Ines with his head lowered. He says that he is ashamed and sorry, and that he will work to pay his debts, and Ines believes him.

Before the painting is taken away, the officer lets Gideon stand in front of it for a few minutes. The old man touches the air above the heron's eye, laughs at the tiny white fleck, and then he weeps.
Tamsin writes quickly in her notebook at the end of the table. She says that she will write the true story of the lodge, and she thanks Ines for finding her in the cold store.
Mrs Bright pours the tea while Mr Bell mends a rope on the porch. They talk about the future of the lodge, and about a new boat for the island.
Marta puts the will on the table and tells everyone what it says. The lodge will go to the Tern Rock Lifeboat, as Orla wished, and Felix will receive his aunt's letter.
Before she leaves, Ines stands in the study and looks at the copy above the fire. Then she lays her hand on the clock in the hall and says a quiet goodbye to Orla.
In the afternoon Ines leaves Tern Rock, walking across the dry causeway in bright sunshine. The lodge will go to the lifeboat as Orla wished, and The Grey Heron will hang there again.
C1C2: On a windswept Friday afternoon, Ines Calloway walked down to the shore from the village station with a single suitcase and a faint sense of foreboding. Before her, across a mile of glistening sand, lay Tern Rock, a dark island crowned by the chimneys of an old stone lodge. She had come to value its paintings for the insurers, and she expected nothing more dangerous than damp.

A battered old car came rattling along the shore road and stopped beside her with a groan of tired brakes, and from it climbed a broad, weathered man in a waxed coat. He introduced himself as Mr Bell, caretaker and boatman to Tern Rock Lodge, and he lifted her suitcase as though it weighed nothing at all. The sea road, he warned her, was open only at low tide, and the tide waited for no one.

He led her to a row of tall white posts standing in the sand, each one banded with paint to show the height of the water. The causeway to the island, he explained, disappeared beneath the sea twice every day, and in a gale it could vanish for far longer. Ines, who disliked surprises and trusted only what she had checked herself, filed the information away with some care.

Then the old car lurched onto the stones, and the whole world seemed to narrow to a single grey ribbon of road with the sea lapping softly on either hand.
