The wet sand shone like pewter in the thin light, and the wheels hissed through shallow pools left behind by the retreating water. Far out on the horizon, a bank of dark cloud was piling slowly upwards, like a second and more menacing sea.

At last the road climbed out of the water, and Tern Rock Lodge rose before them on the crown of the island, a long grey house of weathered stone with tall chimneys and small, deep windows. Salt had streaked its walls and scoured its roof, and a single lamp burned in an upper room, as if the house were keeping watch. It looked, Ines thought, like a place built to withstand everything except its own secrets.

Below the lodge a stone jetty reached out into a tiny harbour, where gulls wheeled and cried above the mast of a single boat. Mr Bell pointed with evident pride to the little blue craft and to the boathouse beside it, which crouched at the water's edge like a dark stone chapel. When the sea road closed, he said, that boat was the island's only link with the mainland.

At the lodge door stood Orla Venn, its owner, leaning on a silver-topped stick and smiling as though she had been expecting trouble and welcomed it. She was seventy years old, small and upright, with white hair and a pair of bright, quick eyes that missed nothing. Ines liked her at once, which was rarely a good sign for a woman in her profession.

Orla swept her inside, past a coat stand heavy with damp oilskins, into a wide hall where a tall clock ticked and warm voices drifted from the lounge. The other guests had all arrived before her, she explained, and would be delighted to be introduced in due course. Ines noticed that the old woman used the word delighted the way other people use the word warned.

In the warm kitchen, a stout woman with floury forearms and shrewd grey eyes poured Ines a cup of tea so strong that it could have supported a spoon. This was Mrs Bright, the cook, who informed her that the larder was full to the rafters and the lodge could survive a siege of a week. A storm was coming, she added, and storms on Tern Rock had a way of keeping visitors far longer than they planned.

Orla drew Ines into a quiet corner of the hall and explained, in a low voice, that she was about to sell the lodge and every painting in it. She had hired Ines to inspect the collection for the insurers, she said, and she wished to hear the truth about every canvas, however unwelcome it might be. Ines, noting the unusual stress on the word truth, promised that she would look closely.

Orla paused beside the tall grandfather clock in the hall and laid a hand on its dark wooden case, almost tenderly. Her late husband had wound it every Friday evening for forty years, she said, and since his death she had taken over the duty herself. It had never lost a minute, and she did not intend to let it begin now.

Orla led her across the hall and into a small study lined from floor to ceiling with leather-bound books, where a lamp glowed on the desk. Above the fireplace hung the lodge's greatest treasure, and she presented it with the air of a woman introducing an old friend. It was called The Grey Heron, she said, and she would not have swapped it for any other painting in the world.

The painting showed a lone bird standing in the shallows at dawn, its long neck folded and its reflection trembling in the water. Every grey and silver of the morning seemed to have been gathered into that single canvas, and the eye of the bird gleamed with a hard, patient light. It was worth, Orla declared with evident pride, far more than the whole island and every stone of the lodge put together.

In the lounge a handsome man in a bright jacket rose from beside the log fire with the easy grace of someone who had been charming people all his life. This was Felix Venn, Orla's nephew, who kissed his aunt on the cheek and shook Ines's hand a fraction too warmly. His smile was dazzling, though it did not quite reach the shadows beneath his eyes.

Beside him sat Hugh Marlowe, Orla's accountant, a thin man in round glasses who gripped a cup of tea as if it might escape. He spoke at astonishing speed about valuations, taxes and the tangled arrangements of the sale, and he mopped his forehead twice in the space of a minute. Ines, who made a habit of noticing nervous people, noticed him at once, and wondered what he was afraid of.

By the window sat Dr Priya Nair, Orla's physician and oldest friend, a calm woman with silver in her hair and a small black bag at her feet. She greeted Ines in a low, unhurried voice and listened to every reply with complete attention. It occurred to Ines that the doctor was the only person in the room who did not seem to be waiting for something.

Gideon Frost glowered from the depths of a leather armchair, an old painter with a mane of white hair and fingers permanently stained with colour. He had painted The Grey Heron more than forty years ago, Orla remarked, and he had never forgiven the world for admiring it more than anything he had done since. Gideon merely grunted at the news, which Ines suspected was his usual form of greeting to strangers.

Lucas Reyes crossed the room with his hand already outstretched, a smooth man in a pale suit whose smile seemed to have been polished that morning. He was an art dealer, he told her, and he represented the buyer who hoped to acquire the lodge and its collection. His grip was warm and dry, and his eyes travelled over Ines as though he were estimating her value.

In the corner a young woman named Tamsin Reed scribbled in a battered notebook, introducing herself as a journalist who was writing about the lodge and its famous painting. Beside her sat Marta Okoye, Orla's lawyer, a composed woman in a dark suit who studied Ines for a long moment and said almost nothing. Ines counted seven other guests in all, and found that she could not yet decide which of them she trusted.

Mr Bell came in from the garden holding his cap against the wind and stood at the window, studying the sky with the grave look of a doctor reading a chart. A storm was coming, he told the room, and a bad one, and the sea road would be under water well before midnight. Nobody laughed, and somewhere in the hall the clock ticked on as though it had heard the news before anyone else.

Mrs Bright led Ines up a wide staircase whose walls were crowded, from the hall to the first landing, with paintings of the sea. There were stormy skies, tall ships and quiet harbours in tarnished gold frames, and the cook remarked that the late Captain Venn had bought nearly all of them. Ines, running her eye across the collection, felt the familiar flutter of professional interest.

Her bedroom was small and plain, with a narrow iron bed, a washstand and a window that looked out over the jetty and the long ribbon of the sea road. She unpacked her notebook, a small magnifying glass and a heavy torch, and set the torch beside the bed from long habit. Ines had spent six years in the police and six more with the insurers, and she had never yet regretted carrying a torch.

Before dinner she made a first inspection of the smaller paintings that lined the landing, a dozen modest oils in plain frames that had never been properly valued. She examined each one in turn with her glass, noting cracks, stains and signatures in her notebook. They were honest pictures, she decided, worth little in money and a good deal in the affection of the people who had hung them.

Beside the landing window hung a faded photograph of a dozen men in oilskins and cork life jackets, standing proudly before a lifeboat on its slip. A brass plate beneath it named the tall man in the middle as Captain Arthur Venn, Orla's husband, who had commanded the island's lifeboat crew for thirty years. Ines studied his weathered, smiling face and thought that Orla must have loved him very much.

Soon after five, while the others were resting in their rooms, Ines slipped back into the study alone and lit the lamp on the desk. She stood in front of The Grey Heron for a long minute, her head slightly on one side, and tried to name the thing that was troubling her. The bird was as beautiful as before, and yet something in its surface seemed wrong.

Then she noticed how brightly the varnish shone, and when she leaned closer she could smell it, a sharp, clean scent that belonged to a workshop and not to a painting forty years old. She told herself firmly that she was an investigator and not an art expert, and that old varnish might be cleaned and renewed for many good reasons. The explanation was perfectly reasonable, and she did not believe a word of it.

Orla came in, tapping her stick on the floorboards, and asked in her quick way what Ines thought of her treasure. Before Ines could answer, the old woman said lightly that it would be better to look again tomorrow, in the honest light of morning, and then to say exactly what she saw. It was an odd request, and Ines noticed that Orla did not quite meet her eyes as she made it.

By six o'clock the wind had risen to a steady roar, and the first heavy drops of rain began to rattle against the windows like flung gravel. The guests drifted into the lounge as the light failed, and Mrs Bright went from room to room lighting the lamps with a long taper. Outside, the sea had turned the colour of slate and begun to heave and mutter against the rocks below.

From the lounge window Ines watched the waves climbing the causeway stone by stone, until the road itself had vanished beneath a heaving grey sheet of water. Mr Bell, who stood grimly beside her, said that no one would cross it tonight, and probably not before Sunday morning. The island, which had seemed so peaceful that afternoon, had become a small, closed world.

In the hall, Felix lifted the heavy black telephone to his ear, frowned, and put it down again with exaggerated care. The line was dead, he announced, and when the guests took out their mobile phones, not one of them could find so much as a single bar of signal. Tern Rock Lodge had been cut off from the rest of the world, and the dinner gong had not even sounded yet.

At eight o'clock precisely the guests took their places at a long mahogany table laid with heavy silver and a row of tall candles, whose flames bent and trembled in every draught. Mrs Bright carried in tureens of steaming soup, and Mr Bell, in a black jacket that did not quite suit him, moved round the table pouring wine. Outside, the storm leaned against the shutters like an impatient latecomer, demanding to be let in.

Orla sat at the head of the table with Marta Okoye on her right hand, and Ines found herself placed between Gideon Frost and Dr Priya, as though by someone with a sense of humour. Felix sat directly opposite her, flushed and handsome in the candlelight, while Lucas, Hugh and Tamsin filled the remaining places down the long white cloth. From her chair Ines could watch every face at the table, which was precisely what she intended to do.

Hugh Marlowe talked incessantly about taxes, valuations and the date of the sale, his hands fluttering above his plate while his soup went cold in front of him. At last Orla laid a gentle hand over his and asked him, with great kindness, to let the soup be eaten before the arithmetic. Hugh subsided, but his glance darted to the old woman's face as though he were afraid of what he might see there.

Gideon complained loudly, to nobody in particular, that modern painters could no longer draw a bird or a boat, and that the whole art world had been taken over by merchants. Lucas Reyes answered with a smooth joke that made even the old man's mouth twitch, while Tamsin Reed leaned forward and asked a string of questions that nobody wished to answer. Between them the conversation stayed polite, but it was the politeness of people walking across thin ice.

Between the soup and the main course, Orla rose with her glass in her hand and asked for silence, and the clatter of spoons died away. She had decided, she told them in a clear, steady voice, to sell Tern Rock Lodge and all its contents to a buyer from abroad, and Mr Reyes would arrange the details. The words dropped into the room like stones into a well, and everyone seemed to wait for the splash.

Felix put down his spoon so hard that it rang against his plate, and the colour drained from his handsome face. He had always believed that the lodge would be his one day, and now he stared at his aunt with a look in which grief, anger and a sort of panic fought for the upper hand. Ines noted that it was the only moment of the evening in which he had stopped smiling.

Marta Okoye rested her hand on a leather folder beside her plate and said nothing at all, though her eyes flicked once towards Felix and then away. Dr Priya spoke into the silence with a few quiet, sensible words about the weather, and little by little the murmur of conversation returned. Orla promised her nephew a private talk after dinner, and Felix, with visible effort, bowed his head.

The clock in the hall struck the quarter, and Orla announced that an evening as important as this deserved a very special bottle of wine. She had kept it in the cellar for many years, she said, and she meant to open it for a toast to the future of the lodge. Nobody offered to fetch it for her, for it was perfectly clear that she wished to go herself.

She took a heavy iron key from its hook beside the door at the back of the dining room, and walked slowly away into the dim passage that led to the rear of the lodge. Ines heard the tap of her stick on the flagstones, fainter and fainter, until the noise of the wind swallowed it altogether. It was the last time that anyone at that table was to see Orla Venn alive, though of course none of them knew it.

A few minutes later Lucas pushed back his chair, murmured that he must wash his hands, and went out through the door to the hall with an easy, unhurried air. Hugh began to talk about money again, and Mrs Bright came in with the main course, a great dish of roast lamb that scented the whole room. Nobody paid the least attention to the empty chairs, which was exactly what a clever man might have counted upon.

The roast lamb was excellent, but the conversation had lost its savour, and a single empty chair at the head of the table seemed to draw every eye. Felix sulked over his glass, Hugh pecked at his food, and Gideon grumbled that a bottle of wine, however grand, should not take so long to find. The candles guttered in a draught, and the wind outside rose another half-tone, as though the night itself were growing impatient.

In the kitchen, Mrs Bright was lifting a heavy dish from the stove when she heard a dull thump from the back passage, as of something falling on stone. She glanced up at the kitchen clock, which stood at two minutes to nine, and decided that the storm had shifted one of the shutters. She had heard a great many strange sounds in her years at the lodge, and she did not think about this one again until much later.

In the hall the great clock struck nine, slow and solemn, and the last note died away without any sign of Orla. Dr Priya glanced at the door more than once, and Ines saw that the doctor's remarkable calm was beginning to wear thin. Even Felix had stopped sulking, and was looking at the doorway with a faint frown.

At five past nine, every light in the lodge went out at the same instant, and the dining room was plunged into complete darkness. Somebody cried out, a glass toppled and rolled across the cloth, and the wind seemed suddenly to be howling inside the very room. For a moment nobody moved or spoke, and the only sound was the ragged breathing of frightened people.

A moment later a small flame appeared in the doorway to the hall, and Lucas Reyes stepped into the room holding a lit candle high above his head. He had been in the cloakroom, he said lightly, and had been lucky enough to find a candle on his way back through the dark. Ines noticed that he was a little out of breath, and that his pale cuff bore a faint white smudge, and she filed both details away without comment.

Mr Bell fetched a lamp from the kitchen and examined the fuse box in the hall, holding the light close to the rows of little switches. Everything was in order, he reported, which could only mean that the storm had brought down the power line from the mainland. Ines, listening, thought that it was the most natural explanation in the world, and found that this did not comfort her at all.

Ines looked at the empty chair at the head of the table and asked, in a voice that sounded quite calm, where Orla was. Nobody had seen her since a quarter to nine, and as the faces turned slowly towards one another in the candlelight, it became clear that twenty minutes was a long time to fetch a bottle of wine. Dr Priya half rose from her chair, but Ines motioned her to stay, and asked Mr Bell to light the way.

Ines took a candle, Mr Bell took the lamp, and together they entered the long passage behind the kitchen, where the stone walls were cold and beaded with damp. The flames bent and shivered in the draught, and their shadows leaped ahead of them like restless ghosts. Behind them the murmur of voices faded, and there was no sound but the storm and the scrape of their shoes.

At the end of the passage they came to the cellar door, a heavy slab of black oak set deep in the wall. It was shut, and an iron bolt on the outside had been shot firmly home. Ines stared at it for a long moment, because a woman who has gone down for a bottle of wine does not bolt herself in.

She drew back the bolt, which slid with a rusty shriek, and pulled the door open on a breath of cold air smelling of stone and old wine. The lamplight fell down a flight of steep steps and came to rest on a small, still figure at the bottom. It was Orla Venn, lying quite motionless with her silver-topped stick beside her, and one look told Ines that she would never speak again.

Dr Priya hurried down the steps with her black bag and knelt beside the still figure, her fingers searching for a pulse at the throat and then at the wrist. When she looked up, her face in the candlelight was grave and very tired. Orla was dead, she said quietly, and she must have died within a few minutes of her fall.

Ines held her candle close to Orla's slender wrist, where a small gold watch lay with its glass shattered across the face. The hands had stopped at two minutes to nine, and she wrote the time in her notebook with fingers that were not quite steady. It was the one fact in that cold, silent place that no clever liar could ever alter.

Dr Priya pointed to a dark bruise on the old woman's shoulder, just below the collar, and said that the fall itself had killed her. She was a family doctor and not a police surgeon, she added carefully, but the mark looked to her very much like the print of a hard shove. Her voice was quite steady, though she did not look at anyone while she spoke.

Ines climbed back up the steps and studied the iron bolt on the outer face of the door, a thick, old-fashioned piece of metal that moved with a stiff rattle. Nobody could have drawn it from inside the cellar, and nobody who fell downstairs by accident could have shut it behind her. It was the kind of simple fact that turned a sad evening into something much worse.

On the second step, half hidden in shadow, Ines found a heavy iron key, which had clearly slipped from Orla's hand as she fell. That meant that Orla had unlocked the door herself and gone down of her own free will, and that somebody else had shot the bolt behind her afterwards. The picture, though ugly, was at least beginning to acquire edges and a frame of its own.

Ines asked the guests to follow her into the lounge, and when they were all seated among the shadows she closed the door and told them plainly that Orla had not died by accident. Because the sea had cut the island off, she said, no police officer could reach them for many hours, and so she intended to treat the matter as a crime. A dreadful silence followed, broken only by the howl of the wind in the chimney.

Felix leapt up and shouted that she had no right to say such things, and Gideon snorted that an insurance clerk was not a detective, whatever she might imagine. Ines let them finish and then explained, quite calmly, that she had served six years in the police before she joined the insurers, and that she knew how to keep a scene and a record. Marta Okoye, who had not spoken, looked at her for a long moment and gave a small nod.

Mr Bell put on his oilskin coat and went out into the storm to check the boat, taking a lantern and a length of rope. He came back half an hour later, soaked to the skin and grey in the face, and reported that the waves had flung the boat against the boathouse wall and smashed it to pieces. There was no way off the island now, he said, for love or money.

He had also tried the radio that he kept in the boathouse, a battered set that had summoned help on better nights than this one. Sea water had got into its case and ruined it, and it gave nothing but a dull hiss and a smell of salt. Whatever had happened in the cellar, Tern Rock Lodge would have to deal with it alone.

Ines went back down to the cellar with a blanket from the kitchen and covered Orla gently, as though she were merely sleeping. Then she locked the door, put the heavy key into her pocket, and asked everyone to keep within sight of at least one other person. It was not much of a precaution, but on that island it was the only one available.

Ines gathered the guests in the lounge, where a few candles threw uneasy shadows on the walls, and asked each of them to say exactly where they had been at two minutes to nine. She wrote every answer in her notebook and watched every face as it was given, because a person's expression often speaks more truthfully than his words. Six years in the police had taught her that patience was the best weapon in any interview.

Hugh, Gideon, Tamsin, Marta and Dr Priya all said, with varying degrees of indignation, that they had been sitting at the dinner table, and each of them could point to a neighbour who had seen them there. Mr Bell added that he had been moving round the same table with the wine, and Felix muttered that he had spent the entire time staring at his plate and hating the world. It was a tidy set of answers, and Ines trusted it only as far as she could have thrown the table.

Lucas Reyes, leaning back in his armchair with the air of a man at a dinner party, said that he had been in the cloakroom at that moment, and that the lights had failed while he was washing his hands. Everyone agreed that he had left the table, but nobody had seen where he went, and nobody could say how long he had been gone. He smiled at Ines as he finished, and Ines found that she did not enjoy the smile.

On a clean page of her notebook, Ines sketched a plan of the lodge, marking the dining room, the hall, the kitchen and the long passage behind it. The cloakroom lay at the front, beside the great door, while the cellar lay at the very back, beyond the kitchen, and the two could hardly have been farther apart. A man who was truly washing his hands at the front could not also have been at the back of the house.

Below the plan she wrote a short list of those who might gain if Orla died before the sale was signed on Sunday, and she kept it brief because she distrusted long lists. There was Felix, who had expected to inherit the lodge; there was Hugh, whose accounts the buyer's lawyers would examine; and there was Lucas, who had vanished from the table for a quarter of an hour. She put a question mark beside every name, and then sat looking at the page for a long time.

Mr Bell and Ines went through the lodge together with a lantern, trying every door and every window in turn, from the front porch to the scullery. All of them were bolted or locked from the inside, and the shutters had been closed against the storm since the afternoon. No stranger had come in from the night, and no stranger could have gone out into it.

A cold supper had been laid in the lounge, but nobody had any appetite, and the dishes returned to the kitchen almost untouched. Ines asked everyone to lock their bedroom doors and to avoid wandering about the house alone, and she was relieved that no one argued. Even Gideon only grunted, and went upstairs with the slow steps of a man a good deal older than he had seemed that morning.

Alone in her small bedroom, Ines sat on the edge of the bed and turned the matter over in her mind, as she had done in a hundred cases before. Orla had been small and slight, and it would have taken no great strength to push her down a flight of steps, which meant that the list of suspects could not be shortened by muscle. Whoever had done it had been quick, calm and cold enough to bolt the door afterwards.

She slept, in the end, for perhaps an hour, and woke at midnight to the sound of a floorboard creaking somewhere below her. The storm was still battering the lodge, but this was a different noise, soft and cautious, the noise of a person who did not wish to be heard. Ines took her torch, opened her door without a sound, and crept down the dark staircase.

Her torch beam swept across the study and found the door standing open, and a man kneeling beside the desk with a drawer in his hands. It was Felix Venn, and as soon as the light touched his face he dropped the drawer with a crash and bolted past her into the darkness. Ines let him go, because she wanted to know what he had been looking for more than she wanted to catch him.

Saturday dawned grey and sullen, with rain still streaming down the windows and a flat white sky lying heavily on the sea. The guests came down one by one to a silent breakfast, and nobody looked at anybody else, as though each of them feared what the next face might reveal. Mrs Bright's porridge went cold in the bowls, and the great clock in the hall ticked on regardless.

Ines found Felix alone in the lounge, slumped in a chair with his head in his hands and his bright jacket crumpled beyond rescue. He admitted at once that he had been searching the study in the night, and that he had been hoping to find his aunt's new will before anyone else did. His honesty, she thought, was either the mark of an innocent man or the last resort of a clever one.

He owed a very large sum of money, he confessed, to a man in the city who did not forgive late payments, and he had begged his aunt for help only a month before. Orla had refused, kindly but firmly, and had told him that she would not pay for the same mistake twice. He had not slept properly since, and the shadows beneath his eyes were no longer charming.

Ines weighed what she had heard, and saw at once that Felix had a motive of the plainest kind. Yet a man in his position needed his aunt alive until she changed her mind, and the more she thought about it, the less the death of Orla seemed to help him at all. It was a puzzle, and Ines, who disliked puzzles that refused to close, wrote it down.

In the library, Marta Okoye opened her leather folder with a small click and drew out a folded document, which she held carefully by its edges. The new will, she told Ines, left Tern Rock Lodge to the island's lifeboat, and gave Felix nothing more than a modest sum and a letter in his aunt's handwriting. Marta had drawn up the document herself, and she did not enjoy saying what it contained.

Orla had signed it two weeks earlier, Marta continued, in the presence of two witnesses, and she had meant to tell her nephew gently after dinner on Friday. The toast was to have been to the lifeboat and the future of the lodge, and Orla had been looking forward to it more than she cared to admit. It was a small, sad detail, and it explained a good deal about the old woman's cheerful mood at the door.

Dr Priya was sitting by the library window with her black bag on her knees, and when Ines asked her about Orla's health she answered slowly and carefully. Orla had suffered from a weak heart for years, she said, and at their last examination she had told her friend that she might have a year, perhaps a little more. That was why Orla had decided to sell the lodge and put her affairs in order, and she had wanted the whole house to enjoy one last, good evening.

When Ines asked to see the accounts, Hugh Marlowe turned the colour of old paper and finally confessed that he had been borrowing small sums from Orla's money for two years. He had always intended to repay every penny, he insisted, and the sale would have uncovered it, but he had never in his life raised his hand against anyone. His voice cracked on the last word, and Ines found, a little to her annoyance, that she believed him.

In the kitchen, Mrs Bright was scrubbing a heavy pan with a fierceness that suggested she was washing away more than burnt gravy. She told Ines that she had been in and out of the dining room with dishes all through the dinner, and that every single time she came in, Mr Marlowe had been sitting in his chair, talking about money. She added, without being asked, that she knew a nervous man from a dangerous one, and that he was nervous.

Ines stood alone in the hall for a minute, listening to the slow tick of the clock and remembering the way Orla had asked her to look at the Heron in the honest light of morning. The rain had slackened a little, and a thin grey gleam was creeping through the study window and across the floorboards. She crossed the hall, pushed open the door, and went in to look at the painting again.

Ines asked Gideon to follow her into the study, and she pulled back the heavy curtains so that the pale morning light fell full upon the canvas. The old man walked up to The Grey Heron, peered at it with his nose almost touching the paint, and then drew back with a sharp breath. It was not his painting, he said in a hoarse voice, and he would stake his life on it.

Gideon sank slowly into the nearest chair, as if his legs had suddenly given way, and told her that he had painted the Heron forty years ago in a rented room beside the sea. He had worked on it through an entire winter, with a stove that smoked and a window that would not shut, and Orla had bought it from his first exhibition when he had not a coin to his name. It was the best thing he ever did, he said, and the only thing that anyone remembered.

Every painter, Gideon explained, leaves a mark that only he can see, and his was a tiny white fleck in the eye of the bird, left by a slip of the brush. He had meant to paint it out the next morning, but when he came back to the canvas he found that the fleck gave the eye a living spark, and he had never dared to touch it. In forty years he had told almost nobody, and he told Ines now with a defiant glare.

Ines took her magnifying glass from her pocket and held it over the dark eye of the painted bird, moving it slowly to catch the grey light. She searched every corner of the eye, and then the whole of the head, and then the water around it, but not a single white fleck was to be found. The bird gazed back at her with a flat and curiously empty stare, as though it knew itself to be a fraud.

Together they lifted the heavy frame from its hook and turned the painting around, and the back of it told its own plain story. The stretcher was pale and modern, the tacks were bright and untarnished, and the sharp smell of fresh varnish rose from the canvas like a confession. Ines had seen enough forgeries in six years with the insurers to recognise one when it was held up to the light.

Gideon was shaking with fury, an old man wounded in the one place where he had never been wounded before, and he could hardly find his words. Somebody had copied his work, he said, and copied it badly, and had not even noticed the fleck that was the soul of the whole thing. Dr Priya, who had come in quietly behind them, laid a gentle hand on his arm and led him to a chair beside the fire.

Ines stood in the middle of the study and let the full meaning of the discovery settle upon her, slowly and heavily, like a coat. The real Grey Heron, a painting worth a very large fortune, had been stolen from this room, and a clever fake had been hung in its place to hide the theft. Somewhere in the lodge, or on the island, there was a thief, and quite possibly he was also a killer.

Mrs Bright was fetched from the kitchen, wiping her hands on her apron, and she said that she had dusted the study on Thursday morning as she always did. The painting had looked just as it always looked, she said, though she would not have known a copy from a masterpiece if the two had been hung side by side. If it had been changed, she added with a certain grim satisfaction, it had been changed after she had gone.

Mr Bell leaned in the study doorway and scratched his chin slowly, a sure sign that he was deciding whether a memory was worth sharing. He had heard somebody moving about in this room late on Thursday night, he admitted at last, and he had assumed that it was Orla, who often could not sleep. He had not looked in, and he now looked at the floor as though it had accused him.

Ines wrote four names on a clean page of her notebook and stared at them for some time. Only those who had slept at the lodge on Thursday night could have changed the canvases: Felix, Hugh, Gideon and Lucas, who had all arrived before the others. Dr Priya, Marta and Tamsin, and indeed Ines herself, had come on Friday, when the copy was already hanging in its place.

Ines knelt in front of the painting and ran her torch along the skirting, where she found a row of pale scrapes in the floorboards, as if the legs of a ladder had stood there. On the window sash there was a smear of fresh varnish, which suggested that somebody had opened the window to blow away the telltale smell. The thief, she reflected, had been careful and clever, but not quite careful enough to leave no trace behind.

She traced the old wooden frame with her fingertips and saw that it was the Heron's own, with its familiar chips and its worn gilding, and that no new marks had been made upon it. The thief had therefore taken only the canvas and left the frame, which meant that he had worked quickly, quietly and with a good deal of skill. It also meant that the forged copy had been painted to exactly the right size.

In the hall, the visitors' book lay open under a lamp, and Ines turned back its pages until she found the entries for the month. Three weeks earlier, Lucas Reyes had spent a whole afternoon in the study, measuring the Heron for his client, and the date was written in his own neat and elegant hand. A forger, she thought, would need exactly those measurements to paint a copy that would fit the frame so perfectly.

Lucas stood before the lounge fire with one hand in his pocket and heard her out with perfect good humour. The painting had been genuine when he valued it, he said, and anyone who wished to steal it would need a skilful forger, a quiet week and a great deal of nerve. His voice was so reasonable that Ines almost forgot to notice how closely he had described the crime.

Felix leaned against the library bookcase and laughed, though not happily, when Ines asked him about the study on Thursday night. He knew the house better than anyone, he agreed, and he had certainly been short of money, but he was no thief and he would not have known whom to sell a stolen masterpiece to. It was a feeble defence, and yet the sheer feebleness of it somehow made it more convincing.

Tamsin Reed caught Ines in a corner of the hall and spoke in a low, rapid voice, hugging her notebook to her chest as though it might be taken from her. She had come to the island, she confessed, because of a tip about copied paintings turning up in country houses whose collections had been valued by Reyes Fine Art. She had not mentioned it to anyone, she said, and she asked Ines not to mention it either.

Mr Bell took Ines on a tour of the kitchen quarters, through the vast larder where sacks of flour stood like sleeping soldiers, and into the cold store, where hams hung from iron hooks. The cold store had a heavy white door with a handle on the outside only, and Mr Bell remarked, with a shiver, that a man could freeze in there before anyone heard him. Ines noticed the door, and noticed that she had noticed it, which was how she knew that it would matter later.

Mrs Bright, wiping her hands on her apron, said that Orla had come up from the cellar at four o'clock on Friday afternoon, and that she had looked as pale as a candle. She had said nothing to anyone, not even a word about the tea that Mrs Bright pressed upon her, and she had gone straight to her room. In all the years the cook had known her, Orla had never before refused a cup of tea.

Ines sat alone in the empty lounge with her notebook open on her knee, tapping her pen against the page. Something in the cellar had frightened or angered Orla at four o'clock on Friday, and by nine that evening she was dead at the foot of the steps. The question was what she had seen there, and what she had decided to do about it.

Mrs Bright hovered in the kitchen doorway as though she wished to say more, but with Mr Bell and two guests nearby she only shook her head and returned to her pans. Ines took a lantern and walked to the end of the kitchen passage, where the black oak door of the cellar stood waiting. She resolved to examine the place properly in daylight, before anyone else had the chance to touch it.

Mrs Bright drew Ines into the pantry among the shelves of jars and shut the door behind them, and she spoke in the low voice of a woman who knew she was risking a good deal. Mr Reyes, she said, had not come back from the cloakroom on Friday night, because she had seen him come out of the kitchen passage with her own eyes. She had kept silent all morning for fear of being wrong about a guest, but her conscience had given her no rest.

She had also heard a heavy bump from the back passage at two minutes to nine by the kitchen clock, she said, and she had told herself that it was the storm moving a shutter. She had been telling herself so ever since, and every time she did, the explanation grew thinner. Ines wrote the time in her notebook, and wrote beside it the single word thump.

The only candles and matches anywhere near the cellar, Mrs Bright went on, were kept in the dresser that stood against the passage wall, within an arm's reach of the cellar door. When the lights failed she had groped her way to the kitchen door, and by the first flare of a match she had seen a man come out of the passage with a candle already burning. He had walked straight into the hall without a word, and he had not once looked round.

Ines held up her wristwatch and walked from the dining room to the cloakroom and back again, and then from the dining room to the cellar door and back, counting the seconds under her breath. Either journey, she found, took a little under two minutes at an ordinary pace. A man who left the table at ten to nine would therefore have had ample time to reach the cellar door before two minutes to nine, and to meet Orla there.

She then went round the hall and examined every candle holder in turn, and every one was cold, clean and unlit, with no trace of melted wax. There was no spare candle on the hall table or the stand, nor on the shelf in the cloakroom, where only a row of coat hooks and a bowl of safety pins awaited her. Wherever Lucas Reyes had found his candle, it had not been in the front of the house.

She found Lucas in the lounge and asked him to sit with her at a small table by the window, where the light was grey and honest. He repeated that he had been in the cloakroom, and added, with a pleasant frown of effort, that he had picked up a candle from the hall table on his way back. His voice did not waver, and neither did the smile, which Ines was beginning to find tiresome.

Ines told him quietly that the hall table held no candle, that the hall holders were all unlit, and that Mrs Bright had seen him come out of the kitchen passage with a flame in his hand. Lucas spread his hands in a gesture of gentle regret and said that the poor woman was surely mistaken in the dark, and that nobody on earth could prove otherwise. He said it so pleasantly, and with such perfect courtesy, that it was almost an insult.

Then he rose to his feet and looked down at her with an expression of kindly warning, as one might look at a child who had picked up something sharp. She was an insurance investigator, he reminded her, and careless accusations had a way of ruining the people who made them as well as the people who were accused. He bowed slightly, and left her alone with the grey window and the slow tick of her own thoughts.

When the door had closed behind him, Ines sat very still and went back over the moment on Friday night when he had come in with his candle held high. There had been a pale smudge on the cuff of his sleeve, a white streak of dust, and she knew at last what it reminded her of. It was exactly like the whitewash that covered the walls beside the cellar steps.

Ines took the heavy key from her pocket, unlocked the cellar door, and went down the stone steps with Mr Bell at her shoulder and a lantern in each of their hands. A grey thread of daylight fell through a small grating high in the back wall, and by its light the cellar looked smaller and plainer than it had in the dark. It was only a cold room full of wine, and yet somebody had died in it.

By the thin grey light of the grating, the cellar looked smaller and colder than it had by candle, a low, whitewashed vault that smelled of stone and old wine. At the foot of the steps lay the shape under its blanket, and Ines stood beside it for a moment in silence, as one does. Then she took out her notebook, because grief, however sincere, could not be allowed to cloud her eyes.

Rows of dusty bottles lay in racks along the walls, every one with its own coat of grey, and the dust on all of them was smooth and undisturbed. Not one bottle had been drawn out, and not one stood on the floor or the steps, so it was plain that Orla had never reached the wine she had come to fetch. The special bottle, then, had been an excuse offered to the dining room, and not her true errand.

Behind the last rack, in the darkest corner of the vault, Ines noticed a large shape standing upright under a white sheet, which had been tucked and pinned with unusual care. She drew the sheet aside with one swift movement, and a heavy gold frame emerged from the shadows, empty and gleaming faintly like a mirror without a face. It was a handsome thing, and it had no business in a wine cellar.

On the back of the frame a paper label had been pasted, printed in small, neat, expensive type, which Ines carried to the grating so that she could read it. It said Reyes Fine Art, and beneath the name were a number, a line of handwriting and a date from the week before. She read it twice, and then she read it a third time, though she had understood it perfectly the first time.

Ines drew her tape measure from her pocket and measured the frame from corner to corner, and then she turned to her notebook, where she had written down the size of the Heron's frame that morning. The figures were exactly the same, to the last fraction of an inch, which was not a coincidence but a method. Somebody had made a copy to fit the painting and had brought it to the lodge in this very frame.

Standing alone with the empty frame, Ines began to see the whole thing as a picture. The forgery had come to the lodge inside this gold frame and had been hidden in the cellar until the thief was ready to make the exchange, and afterwards the empty frame had been covered and left behind. Orla had come down to the cellar on Friday afternoon, perhaps for wine, and what she found there had turned her pale.

Near the foot of the steps a patch of whitewash had been rubbed from the wall, at about the height of a man's shoulder, and a trail of fine white powder lay on the stone beneath it. Somebody had pressed hard against that wall, and recently, for the dust was still loose and bright. Ines thought of a pale sleeve and a streak of white on a cuff, and her pulse quickened.

She explained to Mr Bell, step by step and in a low voice, what she believed had happened in that cold place on Friday evening. Orla had come down again that evening, with her key and her stick and her excuse of the wine, to look at the frame once more, and someone had followed her to the cellar door. There had been a quarrel at the head of the steps, and a push, and a fall, and then the bolt.

Mr Bell listened with his arms folded and his weathered face growing graver by the minute. Then he pointed out, with his usual practical sense, that the real painting could not have left the island, because nobody could have crossed the sea since Friday evening. It must be somewhere in the lodge or on the rocks, he said, and it was only a matter of finding it.

Ines took a folded list from her pocket and put a firm tick beside the first line. They would search the whole lodge, she decided, from the attics to the scullery, and every guest's room as well, with each guest's permission. If anyone refused, that refusal in itself would be well worth writing down in her notebook.

In Felix's room, a bright jacket lay across the bed, and the desk was heaped with unpaid bills, final warnings and a pawn ticket for a gold watch. Ines searched the wardrobe, the drawers, the space under the bed and the chimney, and found a great deal of debt but no painting. It was impossible not to feel sorry for the man, even though she did not trust him.

Hugh Marlowe's room was as tidy as his account book, which lay open on the table beside an unfinished letter to Orla promising to repay every penny of what he owed. There was no canvas in the room, rolled or flat, nothing but a nervous man's neat list of his own mistakes. He stood in the doorway all the while, wringing his hands, and thanked her twice for not being angry.

Gideon's room smelled of linseed oil and old tobacco, and his sketchbooks lay open on the unmade bed, page after page of studies of herons standing in water. In every one of them the eye had been carefully drawn, and in every one a tiny white fleck had been marked with a ring, as a surgeon marks the place for his knife. Whatever else the old man might be, Ines thought, he had remained faithful to his bird for forty years.

Dr Priya's room was austere and tidy, with a row of medicine bottles on the washstand and her worn leather bag standing like a sentry beside the door. She handed Ines, without being asked, a letter that Orla had written to her a year before, which thanked her with great warmth for always telling the truth. Ines read it in silence and handed it back, and neither of them said anything for a moment.

Marta Okoye's room held neat piles of legal papers, a pair of reading glasses and a spare copy of the new will, which Marta produced from her case with a small, dry smile. She stood in the doorway with folded arms while Ines searched, and she remarked that in her profession one learned to be searched with dignity. There was no painting, and Ines felt that there had never been going to be.

Tamsin Reed refused to open her notebook, but she agreed to let Ines listen to the small recorder that she had left running on the dinner table. The recording caught every clink and murmur of the evening, and when Ines played it back she heard that Lucas Reyes did not speak a single word between ten to nine and the moment the lights failed. At two minutes to nine, faint and far away behind the wind, there was a heavy thump.

Lucas's room was almost too tidy, with every shirt folded, every shoe in a line, and the bed made as if for an inspection. His pale suit hung on a hook behind the door, and when Ines touched the right sleeve she found the cuff damp, as though somebody had sponged it in the night. She said nothing, and slipped the observation into her mental notebook beside the others.

Lucas leaned in the doorway of his room with his hands in his pockets, smiling pleasantly, and watched her search his drawers as if she were a guest looking for a lost glove. He thanked her for her trouble when she had finished, and said that he hoped she had found everything she wanted. It was impossible to tell whether he was joking, and that, Ines supposed, was exactly his intention.

In the afternoon Mr Bell and Ines searched the attic, the garden sheds, the boathouse and the end of the jetty, working through cobwebs, fishing nets and broken chairs. They found a great deal of dust and the miserable remains of Mr Bell's boat, and nothing that resembled a stolen masterpiece. The wind had at last begun to drop, and the gulls had returned to the roof.

At dusk, as Ines was climbing the hall stairs with a heavy heart, Tamsin Reed slipped out of the shadows and plucked at her sleeve. She whispered, with a nervous glance over her shoulder, that very early that morning, long before it was light, she had seen Lucas Reyes standing beside the tall clock in the hall. Ines stopped where she was, one foot on the stair, and felt the whole case turn over like a card.

Tamsin sat on the lowest stair with her arms wrapped round her knees and spoke so quietly that Ines had to lean close to hear. She had woken long before dawn, she said, and crept down to write in the lounge, and from there she had seen Lucas Reyes opening the little door in the case of the clock. He had not seen her, and she had not dared to breathe, even when he glanced once towards the stairs.

She had said nothing earlier, she explained, because she was frightened of him, and because a journalist who accuses an art dealer without proof is a journalist who will soon be looking for work. But a woman was dead, and she could not bear to keep quiet any longer. Ines saw that her hands were shaking, and respected her for speaking in spite of it.

Ines took Tamsin gently by the arm and told her to stay exactly where she was, and to say nothing to anyone. She would fetch Mr Bell and a lantern, she promised, and then the three of them would open the clock together, in front of a witness. Tamsin nodded obediently, and Ines went away believing that the matter was safely in hand.

Tamsin Reed, however, had never been good at waiting for other people to act, and as soon as Ines had gone she rose from the stair. She crossed the dim hall on tiptoe, one hand trailing along the wall, towards the tall clock whose slow tick seemed to grow louder at every step. She told herself that she only wanted a look, and that nobody would ever know.

On her way to find Mr Bell, Ines heard a furious quarrel erupt in the lounge, where Felix and Gideon were accusing each other of lies while Hugh stood anxiously between them with his hands raised. She could not leave an argument like that to burn, for there was no telling what a shouting man might say or do. It took her a good ten minutes to calm them both, and she did not like the delay.

As the shouting died away, Ines heard another sound, faint and irregular and muffled by walls, a banging that seemed to come from the back of the house. She ran back to the hall, found the stairs empty and the clock ticking placidly in its corner, and knew with a cold certainty that something had gone wrong. She followed the noise towards the kitchen at a run, with her heart hammering in her ears.

The banging led her and Mr Bell, who had come running at her call, to the cold store, where the heavy white door had been wedged shut with a kitchen chair jammed under the handle. Mr Bell wrenched the chair away and swung the door open, and a gust of freezing air rolled out across the floor. Inside, among the hanging hams, a small figure was crouching with her fists raw from beating on the wood.

Tamsin stumbled out into the light of the kitchen, shaking with cold and fear, her teeth chattering so hard that she could not speak. Dr Priya, who had been fetched by Mrs Bright, wrapped her in a blanket and sat her down beside the warm black stove, holding both of her hands in her own. For several minutes nobody asked her anything, and the only sound was the hiss of the kettle.

When at last she could speak, Tamsin said that she had opened the little door in the clock and found a long, stout cardboard tube lying inside, and that she had barely touched it when somebody seized her from behind. A hand clamped over her mouth, she said, and she was pushed along the passage and into the cold store, and the door slammed before she could scream. She had seen nothing of her attacker but the edge of a pale sleeve.

Ines hurried to the hall with a candle and opened the little door in the case of the tall clock, kneeling to peer in among the weights and the swinging pendulum. There was nothing inside but dust and the dull brass gleam of the mechanism, and the tube that Tamsin had seen was gone. Whoever had taken it had been quick, and had probably been watching her all along.

Ines asked every guest where they had been during the ten minutes of the quarrel in the lounge, and the answers came back clear and tidy. Felix and Gideon had been shouting at one another before Hugh and herself, Marta and Dr Priya had been together in the library, and Mrs Bright had been upstairs making the beds. Only Lucas Reyes could say merely that he had been walking alone, and nobody could confirm it.

That evening, when the candles were lit, Ines took down the printed table of tides that hung beside the barometer in the hall and studied it by the flame. The storm surge had kept the sea high all through Saturday, but the figures showed that the sea road would stand clear of the waves at twenty to five on Sunday morning. She wrote the time in her notebook and underlined it twice, as if the line itself might hold the tide to its promise.

Mr Bell, who had been watching the weather like a sailor all day, tapped the glass of the barometer and nodded slowly. The wind was dropping, he said, and the pressure was beginning to rise, and unless the sea played a trick on them the road would open exactly as the table promised. He said it with the quiet confidence of a man who had lived all his life by the tide.

Ines spread a rough map of the island on the kitchen table, weighing down the corners with salt cellars, and she thought aloud while Mr Bell watched. The tube was no longer in the lodge, she reasoned, because the clock had been the last of the hiding places and Lucas knew that the lodge might be searched again. He must have hidden it somewhere outside, among the rocks or the outbuildings, where he could fetch it at the moment he chose to run.

Lucas could not leave the island until the sea road opened, Ines explained in a low voice, and he would want to be across it long before the police arrived to ask questions. That gave him one night, and a single narrow window in which to collect the tube and run. She told Mr Bell, Felix and Dr Priya what she planned to do about it, and by the end of her explanation all three of them were nodding.

Felix, who had listened in silence with his chin lifted, said that he wanted to make up for his foolishness, and that he would do whatever she asked. Ines studied him for a long moment, weighing the debts, the lies and the dazzling smile against the plain look in his tired eyes, and then she held out her hand. He shook it as though it were the first honest thing he had done in a year.

Ines found Mrs Bright by the stove, stirring a pot of broth that nobody would eat, and asked her in a whisper to leave the back door unbolted and the kitchen dark that night. The cook gave her a long, shrewd look, and then nodded once, without asking a single question. In her experience of the world, she remarked, a woman who asked for a thing like that had a good reason.

At supper in the lounge, Ines announced in a clear voice that Mr Bell would cross the sea road at first light and bring the police back with him. Nobody would be allowed to leave the island, she added, until every bag and every pocket had been searched. She said it lightly, as though it were a mere detail, and she did not look at any one face in particular.

Lucas Reyes lifted his cup of tea and held it before him without drinking, as though he had forgotten what it was for. His finger tapped the rim, once and then again, and the china made a small ringing sound in the silence of the room. Ines, who was looking carefully at the fire, heard it and was perfectly satisfied.

Dr Priya took Tamsin upstairs to her own room, where the two women could lock the door and sleep within reach of one another, and she promised to keep the key in her hand all night. The others lingered by the fire, yawning, uneasy and glancing over their shoulders at every shadow. Everything was ready now, and there was nothing left for Ines to do except wait.

The guests sat round the lounge fire in a loose circle, listening to the long slow ticking of the clock in the hall and pretending to be at ease. Lucas Reyes talked politely about the weather, the tides and the difficulties of travel in autumn, in the tones of a man at a country house party. Nobody answered him with much enthusiasm, and Ines, from her corner, thought that he seemed almost to enjoy the silence.

Gideon stared into the flames and began, quite unexpectedly, to tell a story about Orla and her husband. Long ago, he said, the young couple had bought the Heron from a very poor painter for almost nothing, and they had hung it over their first fire in a cottage that leaked. The old man's gruff voice softened as he went on, and he did not seem to notice that the room had fallen silent to listen.

Marta said, after a pause, that Orla had chosen the lifeboat because its crew had carried her husband's coffin ten years before, and had never allowed her to feel alone since. Every Christmas, she added, they came to the lodge with a basket of fish and a bottle of rum, and Orla would pretend to scold them for tracking sand across the hall. It was the only time that evening when anyone smiled, and Ines was glad to see it, even for a moment.

Hugh Marlowe sat very straight in his chair and wrote quickly on a sheet of lodge notepaper, his pen scratching in the stillness. He told Ines, without lifting his head, that he would give the buyer's lawyers a full confession in the morning, and that he would repay every penny if it took him the rest of his life. His voice shook, but the pen did not, and he went on writing until the page was full.

By midnight the rain had stopped altogether, and the wind that had screamed round the chimneys for two days began to sink into long, uneven sighs. The sound of the sea beyond the rocks changed too, from a wild roar to a deep, slow breathing, as though some great animal were falling asleep. Ines heard the change and knew exactly what it meant for her plan, and for the long night ahead.

One by one the guests took their candles and climbed the stairs, murmuring goodnight in low voices that did not carry far. Lucas Reyes was the last to rise, stretching with a lazy yawn and wishing everyone a pleasant night in his smooth, pleasant voice before strolling away towards his room. Ines watched his back until it vanished round the turn of the stair, and then she let out a slow breath.

Ines slipped into the kitchen, where the fire had sunk to a bed of red embers, and sat in the dark beside the window with her notebook shut upon her knee. She did not light a candle, and she kept her breathing slow and quiet, as she had learned to do on long nights in the police. In the hall the great clock struck twelve, and she listened to the echo fade into the stones.

Mrs Bright, who had crept in on slippers to leave a flask of hot tea and a currant bun on the table, whispered a blessing and returned to her bed without a sound. The clock struck one, and a long, cold hour began, in which nothing in the lodge moved at all. Ines drank the tea in small sips and found that it was exactly as strong as she needed.

Outside, in the sharp air, Mr Bell and Felix crouched together beside the back path under an old tarpaulin, with a lantern hidden under a folded cloth. Felix, who was not used to waiting in the cold, kept his teeth clenched to stop them chattering, and Mr Bell, who was, said nothing at all. Between them lay a coil of rope that the boatman had brought, just in case.

At two o'clock the clock in the hall struck again, and Ines heard the last of the wind die away among the chimneys. Through the kitchen window she could see a few stars between the thinning clouds, small and hard and very far away. She flexed her cold fingers, listened to the silence of the sleeping house, and went on waiting.

At three o'clock in the morning, when the lodge was deepest in its sleep, a stair creaked somewhere above her in the dark. Ines held her breath and sat perfectly still, and the sound came again, soft and slow and cautious, followed by another step and then another. Someone was coming down, and he was taking great trouble not to be heard.

A figure in a long coat tiptoed into the kitchen and crossed the flagstones within a yard of the pantry door behind which Ines was hiding. It was Lucas Reyes, and he moved like a man who had made up his mind, easily and without pause, as he drew back the bolt of the back door. A breath of cold night air came in, the door closed softly behind him, and he was gone.

Ines slipped off her shoes and followed him out into the cold, keeping close to the wall of the lodge, where the shadows were deepest. Mr Bell rose from beneath his tarpaulin and fell in beside her without a word, while Felix, at a sign from Ines, ran ahead along the shore to a hiding place among the rocks. The three of them had rehearsed it in the kitchen, and now it was going exactly as planned.

Lucas followed the narrow path among the black rocks, with a small torch that he held low and pointed at his feet. Overhead, a few faint stars shone through the broken clouds, and the sea hissed and sucked at the stones on either side of him. He did not look back once, and that, Ines thought, was the mark of a man who believed himself alone.

The path led down to the boathouse, a squat building of dark stone crouching at the water's edge, with its great door hanging half open on a broken hinge. Lucas slipped inside, and Ines and Mr Bell crept along the wall in his wake, until they could stand on either side of the doorway and look in. The air inside smelled of tar, weed and wet rope, and the water slapped softly beneath the floor.

Inside, the beam of the torch moved slowly over the ruined hull of Mr Bell's boat, which lay on its side on the slip with its planks stove in. Lucas set down the torch, reached into the wreck beneath a broken seat, and drew out a long, stout cardboard tube, which he held for a moment against his chest like a child. It was exactly the tube that Tamsin had described, and Ines felt a quiet thrill of triumph.

Mr Bell raised a heavy fist to rush in, but Ines caught his sleeve and shook her head. Beneath the boathouse floor the water of the slip was deep and black, and a man cornered in the dark could drop his burden into it in a moment. She wanted him out in the open, on the shallows, where nothing could be lost for ever.

Lucas tucked the tube under his arm, picked up the torch, and walked out of the boathouse by the seaward door, past the rocks and down towards the shore. He passed within thirty paces of the two silent watchers and did not turn his head, because his mind was already on the road ahead. Ines let him go a little way, and then she followed, step by careful step.

The storm had passed completely now, and the clouds were tearing apart above the island to show the stars in great clean spaces. Below the rocks the dark water was sliding back from the land, and the first stones of the causeway were beginning to show, shining wetly like the backs of sleeping animals. In the starlight the sea road lay across the bay like a pale ribbon.

Lucas stopped at the very edge of the sea and looked at his watch by the thin light of his torch, and then he switched the torch off. He was waiting for the tide to fall, and Ines, crouching behind a rock fifty paces behind him, was waiting for the very same thing. Beside her, Mr Bell breathed slowly through his nose, and the sea breathed with him.

The sea went down slowly, as though reluctant to give up its hold on the land, and the black stones of the causeway appeared one by one out of the water. The tall white posts that marked the tide stood up from the shallows like the masts of a drowned ship, each one streaming and shining. Ines watched the road rise from the sea, and counted the minutes in her head as a sailor counts the waves.

Lucas Reyes, who had waited with the patience of a cat, stepped onto the wet stones the moment that they were clear, with the tube clutched tight against his chest. He walked quickly, and the water, still ankle-deep in the hollows, sucked and splashed at his shoes. He had perhaps forty paces of road behind him when Ines stood up from behind her rock.

Ines stepped out onto the causeway behind him, holding the lantern high above her head so that its light spread wide across the water. She had not raised her voice in years, and she was surprised by the steadiness of it as it rang out across the bay. She called his name once, clearly and without the smallest tremor, and the sound seemed to hang over the water for a long moment.

Lucas spun round, and for a moment he stood quite motionless in the glare of the lantern, with his mouth a little open and the tube still pressed to his chest. Ines saw the understanding arrive in his face, quickly and completely, like a light switched on in an empty room. He had been so clever for so long, and he had never once imagined that he might be waited for.

Then he ran, throwing a single wild glance at the dark sea on his left and the dark sea on his right, and pounding away along the causeway with the tube under his arm. But Felix, who had been crouching among the rocks at the foot of the road, sprang up with a shout and flung himself after him, and Mr Bell charged in his wake with his heavy boots thudding. The chase was on, and it went across the open sea in the cold half-light.

The causeway was never meant for running, and the slabs glittered with wet weed and slippery pools, so that every stride was a gamble against a fall. Lucas was fast and desperate, and he gained a few paces, but the road was long and the sea was close, and the spray from the retreating waves flew up around his legs. Behind him, boots splashed and hammered, and the lantern bobbed and swung in Ines's hand.

Halfway across, Lucas realised that he could not outrun them, and he swung back the tube to hurl it far out into the dark sea. Felix, who had spent his whole life being charming and careless, threw himself forward with a cry and tore it from his hands at the very moment of the throw. He fell heavily on the stones, and he clutched the tube to his chest and did not let go.

Lucas wheeled away to run on, but his foot came down on a mat of green weed and flew out from under him, and he crashed full length on the stones with a cry of pain. Before he could rise, Mr Bell was upon him, kneeling on his back with one great hand pinning each wrist, breathing like a bellows. The boatman said nothing, which was, in the circumstances, the most eloquent remark he could have made.

At last Lucas stopped struggling, and a long moment passed in which nobody spoke, and nothing was heard but the slow slap of the waves against the stones. Then he gave a short, bitter laugh, and allowed himself to be helped up and seated on a flat stone at the edge of the road, where he put his head in his hands. The fight had gone out of him completely, and in the lantern light he looked like a tired and rather ordinary man.

The first grey light of dawn crept over the sea, widening slowly along the edge of the horizon, and the clouds in the east took on the colour of pearls. The causeway lay wide and pale before them, a clear road of wet stone running to the mainland, and the little white posts stood along it like sentries. It was, Ines reflected, going to be a beautiful morning, and it was strange to feel so tired.

Mr Bell, who had understood that somebody must fetch the police and that his legs were the best the island possessed, set off along the causeway at a steady run, his heavy boots splashing in the shallows. Ines and Felix remained behind with their prisoner, who sat on his flat stone and stared at the water as though he were reading something written there. Nobody spoke for a long time, and the dawn grew slowly lighter over the quiet and glittering sea.

It was Lucas who spoke first, in a low, tired voice that held none of its former polish. He had stolen the painting, he said, because he owed more money than he could ever repay, and because for years he had been living on the credit of a reputation that was already beginning to crack. The Grey Heron, he had decided, was his one chance to put everything right.

On Thursday night, when the lodge was asleep, he had slipped into the study, lifted the real Heron from its frame, rolled it into the tube he had brought, and hung a copy in its place. The copy had been painted in a week by a forger in the city, working from photographs and from the measurements that he himself had taken, and it had travelled to the lodge in the gold frame. He had hidden the frame in the cellar, planning to take it away before anybody thought of looking there.

Orla, however, had gone down to the cellar on Friday afternoon, and had found the empty gold frame under its sheet. At dinner he had read the truth in her face, he said, in the long look she gave him across the table before she rose, and when she left the room for the wine he had followed. She had been waiting for him at the cellar door, with the key in her hand and her chin high, and she had told him quite calmly that she would call the police in the morning.

He had pushed her, he admitted at last, in a moment of blind panic, and she had fallen backwards down the steps, and he had heard the dreadful sound of it. He had bolted the door without thinking, and stood trembling in the dark scullery for what felt like an hour, until the lights failed and gave him his chance to take a candle from the dresser. Then he had walked back to the dining room, and he did not ask for pity now, and Ines did not offer any.

He said that he was sorry about Tamsin Reed, who had found the tube in the clock at the worst possible moment, and that he had only wanted to keep her quiet until the tide fell. After that he had carried the tube out to the boathouse, because he knew that the lodge would be searched again. He swore that he had never meant to hurt anyone, and Ines told him quietly that Orla Venn's death was a poor proof of it.

Ines knelt on the cold stones of the causeway and pulled the cap from the tube with great care, while Felix held the lantern, though the dawn had already made it unnecessary. She drew out a roll of canvas, soft with age and smelling faintly of linseed, and unrolled it gently across her knees, a hand's breadth at a time. A grey bird stood in silver water, and the real Grey Heron looked up at her out of forty years.

Felix bent closer, and Ines tilted the canvas towards the growing light so that they could both see the eye of the bird. It was dark and deep and gleaming, a living thing in the middle of the painting, and in the exact centre of it sat a tiny fleck of white, no bigger than a grain of salt. It was the one thing that no copyist had thought to look for, and it was the thing that had condemned him.

Felix asked her, in a voice a little hoarse with cold, how she had known it was Lucas, and Ines counted the answer on her fingers. The iron bolt had proved that it was murder, and the stopped watch and the recording had fixed the very minute of it. The candle and the whitewash on his cuff had put him in the passage when he swore he was washing his hands, and he had forged every link of that chain himself.

The sun rose clear of the sea as the police arrived, two officers in bright yellow coats, striding across the causeway with Mr Bell beside them and their boots ringing on the wet stone. Ines told them what she knew, and handed over the tube, and Lucas Reyes rose from his stone without a word and held out his wrists. The sea road, so lately an enemy, lay open and golden behind them, and the long storm was over.

The officers heard her out with growing astonishment, and then the elder led Lucas Reyes away along the causeway to the police car that waited on the far shore. The younger officer walked up to the lodge with Ines and Felix to take their statements, and he looked about him at the quiet grey house with a mixture of respect and alarm. Lucas did not once look back at the island, and the island, in its pale morning light, seemed to take no notice of his going.

In the lounge, over a cup of strong tea, Ines told the young officer everything, from the cellar bolt to the tube in the boathouse, like one who had given evidence before. She handed over her notebook, with every time and every clue set out in her small, upright hand. He read it in silence, and when he had finished, he asked her, in a rather subdued voice, whether she had ever thought of rejoining the police.

At breakfast the sun poured through the lounge windows and lay across the long table in bright squares, and for the first time in two days the guests ate as people who were hungry. Hugh Marlowe rose to his feet with his napkin crumpled in his hand and promised, in a voice that shook, to repay every penny he had borrowed from Orla's money. Nobody laughed at him, and Marta Okoye said briskly that she would help him to arrange it.

Felix stood in front of Ines with his handsome head lowered, like a boy before a headmaster, and said that he was ashamed of the way he had behaved in the study and everywhere else. He would work to pay his debts, he said, and he would not ask anybody for a penny, and he hoped that Orla, wherever she was, could forgive him. Ines, who had seen many liars, looked into his tired face and found that she believed him.

Before the painting was taken away as evidence, the young officer allowed Gideon Frost a few minutes alone with it, and the old man stood before the unrolled canvas with the tears running down his weathered face. He reached out one stained finger towards the eye of the heron, and laughed aloud at the tiny white fleck that had always been his secret. Then he wept again, and Dr Priya took his arm, and nobody said anything at all.

At the end of the table, Tamsin Reed was writing quickly in her notebook, with a cup of tea going cold beside her elbow and the colour back in her cheeks. She intended to write the whole true story of Tern Rock Lodge, she told Ines, and it would not be about a famous painting but about a brave old woman and the people who had cared for her. She thanked Ines, with great simplicity, for coming to find her in the cold store.

Mrs Bright poured tea for anyone who held out a cup, while Mr Bell sat on the porch outside the window, mending a coil of rope with slow, patient fingers. Through the open glass the two of them could be heard discussing the future of the lodge, and a new boat for the island, and whether the sea would ever again be so unkind. It was the ordinary conversation of ordinary people, and Ines found it more comforting than any speech.

When the plates had been cleared, Marta Okoye set her leather folder on the table, took out the will, and told the company in her dry, clear voice what it said. Tern Rock Lodge would go to the island's lifeboat, as Orla had wished, and the crew would decide how best to use it, and Felix would receive his aunt's letter and a modest sum. There was a silence, and then Felix, to everyone's surprise, began quietly to clap.

Before she left, Ines went once more into the study, where the false Heron still hung above the fire and looked, in the morning light, almost embarrassed to be there. Then she crossed the hall and laid her palm for a moment on the dark wooden case of the great clock, which went on ticking as steadily as ever. She said goodbye to Orla in her own way, silently, and promised her that the truth had been told.

That afternoon, Ines walked back across the causeway in bright sunshine, with the sea glittering quietly on either side and the lodge growing small behind her. Orla's wishes would be carried out, Marta had promised, so that the lodge would help the lifeboat that saved sailors and The Grey Heron would hang once more over the study fire. Ines had never known a house so quiet and so clear after a storm.
